channels.title: Four channels, one message
channels.intro: Members learn the union in different places. The facts should match everywhere.

social.label: Social
social.content: Fast updates and member stories. Closed Facebook groups are common — see platforms below.

print.label: Print
print.content: Flyers and handouts for meetings, gates, and members who never scroll. Print Guide for layout.

channels.warning: If the meeting time on the flyer does not match the Facebook post, members stop trusting all four.

platforms.title: Which platforms to choose
platforms.intro: Start with one social channel and do it well. Add others when the first one is sustainable.

facebook.label: Facebook / closed group
facebook.content: Broad reach, events, longer posts. Many locals use a members-only group as the primary channel.

instagram.label: Instagram
instagram.content: Visual storytelling and Reels. Pair with Photo Consent and short-form video guides.

website.label: Website as anchor
website.content: Not a daily feed — a durable contact page and strike FAQ when crisis hits.

startOne.label: Start with one
startOne.content: A dead Instagram beside a lively Facebook group hurts more than having one channel.

platforms.tip: Put the same QR on boards and flyers — it should land on your website or group join link, not a broken short URL.

tone.title: Tone of voice
tone.intro: Write for a steward reading on break — not a comms degree.

we.label: Speak as we
we.content: Our members, our local, our bargaining team — collective voice, not a single officer’s hot take.

honest.label: Honest about setbacks
honest.content: Members forgive bad news they understand. They do not forgive spin.

plain.label: Plain language
plain.content: Cut jargon and acronyms unless your audience uses them daily. Define CA articles when you cite them.

crisis.label: Shorter in crisis
crisis.content: Strike mode: fewer adjectives, one spokesperson, president approves. See the Strike Guide.

frequency.title: Posting frequency and mix
frequency.intro: Consistency beats volume. Members should know roughly when to expect you.

normal.label: Normal times
normal.content: Two or three posts per week is enough for most locals between bargaining rounds.

mix.label: Simple content mix
mix.content: Rough guide: 40% updates, 30% member stories (with consent), 20% education, 10% solidarity.

strike.label: Strike or countdown
strike.content: Switch to the Strike Guide three-messages rhythm — not endless reactive posting.

quiet.label: Quiet weeks are fine
quiet.content: Post only when you have news. An empty page beats noise.

frequency.tip: Batch drafts Sunday night; president approves Monday. Saves panic posts on Wednesday.

trolls.title: Trolls, spam, and management
trolls.intro: Bad-faith comments will come. Your job is to protect the space, not win every thread.

spam.label: Hide spam and harassment
spam.content: Delete slurs and threats. Document screenshots for executive if needed.

management.label: Management accounts
management.content: Respond once with facts and CA language if president approves. No pile-ons.

pin.label: Pin the correction
pin.content: One pinned post beats twenty replies. Link the Strike Guide management section in crisis.

never.label: Never post
never.content: Confidential bargaining, member discipline details, or home addresses — online or in DMs.

trolls.warning: If you are typing angry, hand the draft to another officer or wait for president sign-off.

accessibility.title: Alt-text, contrast, and mobile
accessibility.intro: Shop-floor members use small screens in bright hallways. Design for that.

alt.label: Alt-text on every image
alt.content: Draft in Alt-Text Assistant; paste in the platform alt field, not the caption. Include on-image words.

contrast.label: Contrast before export
contrast.content: Run Brand Kit contrast checks. Pale grey on white fails on phones and copiers.

captions.label: Captions on video
captions.content: Reels and Shorts need captions for members who watch muted at work.

mobile.label: Mobile-first layout
mobile.content: Flyers and graphics: large type, one ask, readable at arm's length — same Glance Test as print.

fullWeek.title: Worked example: a normal comms week
fullWeek.intro: No strike, no bargaining deadline — just keeping the local visible between meetings.

mon.label: Monday — plan
mon.content: Comms lead drafts two posts: Wednesday meeting reminder, Friday member spotlight (consent confirmed). President approves both.

wed.label: Wednesday — meeting push
wed.content: Graphic Maker export to group; Board Notice PDF to cork; same time and room on both.

thu.label: Thursday — board refresh
thu.content: Pull last month’s flyer. Leave contacts and H&S strip up. Add solidarity poster if the board looks bare.

fri.label: Friday — spotlight
fri.content: Post spotlight with alt-text. No location tag. Log consent in officer notebook.

fullWeek.tip: Four touchpoints, one comms lead, zero last-minute scrambles — that is the Blueprint in practice.

contract-enforcement.title: Worked file timeline
contract-enforcement.aria: Day-by-day contract enforcement file from intake to next step
contract-enforcement.caption: Copy the spacing: filter and records before you file, Step 1 on the clock, then a recorded employer answer.

d0.label: Day 0 — member intake
d0.summary: Hear the OT skip story. Request time records. Do not promise a win.

d1.label: Day 1 — contract pull
d1.summary: Read Article 12.04. Run the 5-point filter. Identify payroll custodian.

d2.label: Day 2 — 6 W's + FAR
d2.summary: Interview Maria. Name witnesses. Draft specific WANT: pay plus seniority order.

d3.label: Day 3 — Step 1 or file
d3.summary: Raise informally if required. File written grievance on the CA clock.

d7.label: Day 7 — denial logged
d7.summary: Employer denies. Calendar next step. Brief chief steward.

progressive-discipline.title: Worked file timeline
progressive-discipline.aria: Discipline file from letter intake through grievance
progressive-discipline.caption: Classify the document before the member signs anything. Mitigation and ladder proof before you concede a rung.

d0.label: Day 0 — letter received
d0.summary: Obtain full letter. Flag threat language. Advise member not to sign admissions.

d1.label: Day 1 — classify + demand
d1.summary: Treat as formal discipline. Demand withdrawal of dismissal threat or file.

d2.label: Day 2 — ladder + mitigation
d2.summary: Map prior steps. Gather clean record, training offer, inconsistency proof.

d3.label: Day 3 — meeting
d3.summary: Insist on disclosure. No member speculation. Offer coaching-only resolution.

d7.label: Day 7 — grievance filed
d7.summary: Letter stays on file. Written grievance cites proportionality and ladder skip.

human-rights-accommodation.title: Worked file timeline
human-rights-accommodation.aria: Accommodation file from request through RTW design or grievance prep
human-rights-accommodation.caption: Functional limits only. Log employer silence. Dialogue and grievance prep can run in parallel.

d0.label: Day 0 — request logged
d0.summary: Receive accommodation ask. Block diagnosis fishing. Confirm protected ground.

d1.label: Day 1 — Meiorin + hardship
d1.summary: Walk three steps. Demand cost quote and funding search for desk refusal.

d3.label: Day 3 — employer response
d3.summary: Counter with phased RTW and in-unit task bundling. Name OHRC if morale cited.

d5.label: Day 5 — RTW grid
d5.summary: Propose work-hardening hours tied to functional limits. Set 30-day joint review.

d7.label: Day 7 — stall documented
d7.summary: Three weeks without counter-proposal. Prepare grievance while dialogue continues.

democratic-governance.title: Worked file timeline
democratic-governance.aria: GMM quorum loss from opening headcount through void vote
democratic-governance.caption: Secretary announces every quorum change. Spending motions die with lost quorum.

d0.label: Opening — quorum met
d0.summary: 18 present; quorum 15. Sign-in sheet locked. Chair opens agenda.

d1.label: Mid-meeting — recount
d1.summary: Four leave for bus. Secretary counts 14 — announce lost quorum.

d2.label: Same night — void vote
d2.summary: Charity motion fails for lack of quorum. Discussion may continue; vote cannot.

d3.label: Next step — reschedule
d3.summary: Minutes record time and count. Reschedule vote or mail ballot per bylaws.

financial-health.title: Worked file timeline
financial-health.aria: Reimbursement control from total-only slip through dual signature
financial-health.caption: Itemized receipt and two signers beat urgency every time.

d0.label: Day 0 — slip submitted
d0.summary: President submits $150 total-only credit card slip for executive lunch.

d1.label: Day 1 — refuse sign
d1.summary: Treasurer holds cheque. Demand itemized receipt and trade-union purpose.

d3.label: Day 3 — voucher complete
d3.summary: Itemized food receipt attached. Two authorized signers review and sign.

d7.label: Day 7 — variance note
d7.summary: Trustee flags pattern in next variance report if executive meals repeat.

building-collective-power.title: Worked file timeline
building-collective-power.aria: Organizing file from barrier mapping through grievance and bargaining package
building-collective-power.caption: Grieve active harm now. Bargain systemic fixes for the next round.

d0.label: Week 0 — barrier named
d0.summary: Suburban hall excludes part-time racialized members. Start survey.

d1.label: Week 1 — survey live
d1.summary: Voluntary demographics plus barrier themes. Propose hybrid meeting pilot.

d3.label: Week 3 — active harm
d3.summary: Microaggression pattern reported. File harassment grievance; keep survey running.

d7.label: Week 7 — package draft
d7.summary: Convert survey top barrier into clause + accountability mechanism for bargaining.

unionBoardsGuide.subtitle: Reach members who are not on social. Start with a bare-minimum layout, then add notices and posters.

bareMinimum.title: Bare-minimum board
bareMinimum.intro: Every board should answer: How do I find you online? Who do I call for health and safety? Who is on the LEC? What is happening next?
bareMinimum.tip: Print always-on pieces once on sturdy stock. Refresh only the rotating zone. Fill empty space with solidarity posters so the board never looks abandoned.

header.title: Local header
header.content: Local number, short name, and Brand Kit logo. Print a Board Banner so the cork reads as yours from across the room.

socials.title: Socials and digital link
socials.content: Add one QR code or short URL that points to your site, your group, or this site. One clear call to action (“Get support” or “Follow us”) beats a wall of icons.

healthSafety.title: Health and safety
healthSafety.content: JHSC / H&S contacts, how to report a hazard, and where to find the latest bulletin. Keep phone numbers large and current.

lec.title: LEC and steward list
lec.content: Local Executive Committee roles with names and work contacts (or steward office hours). Update after elections with Org Chart so the cork matches the current names.

events.title: Events or rotating spot
events.content: Membership meetings, bargaining updates, workshops, or a solidarity poster. This is the only zone that should change weekly.

whatToPrint.title: What to print
whatToPrint.intro: Think in layers: permanent identity, standing resources, and a rotating slot.

always.label: Always on the board
always.content: Header/logo, socials QR or URL, health & safety contacts, LEC / steward list.

rotate.label: Rotate often
rotate.content: Meeting notices, bargaining updates, event flyers, and high-energy solidarity posters for empty space.

optional.label: Optional extras
optional.content: Member spotlight (with consent), contract highlight one-pagers, how-to-file-a-grievance tear-offs.

sizes.label: Sizes that work
sizes.content: Letter (8.5×11) for dense contact lists; tabloid (11×17) for notices and posters readable from across the room.

where.title: Where to post
where.content: Use union-designated boards in break rooms, steward offices, and agreed spots. Never post on management boards without permission. Check CA posting rights.

howLong.title: How long to leave notices up
howLong.content: Remove outdated notices promptly. Meetings: post 1-2 weeks ahead, remove after. Bargaining: refresh weekly. Strike: daily. Keep bare-minimum zones current.

whatNot.title: What not to post
whatNot.content: Never post confidential bargaining positions, member home addresses, or internal strategy. Do not name individuals in grievances. Ask your president if unsure.

pairing.title: Pair with social media
pairing.content: Use the same headline on the board notice and social graphic. Post the board first, then share on social with a photo of the posted notice (consent anyone visible).

printGuide.title: Print Communications Guide
printGuide.subtitle: Why print still matters, how to design flyers that work, and how to print on a local budget.
printGuide.intro: Paper still reaches members who never see a post. Use this page to decide when to print, how to design for the shop floor, and how to stretch a small budget. Start with one rally flyer, then post the same headline on the board.

when.title: When to print
when.intro: Print is not a backup for locals that feel behind on digital. It is how you reach people social media never sees, and how you make the union visible in the workplace itself.

divide.label: It bridges the digital divide
divide.content: Not every member has a smartphone, a data plan, or quiet time to scroll. A flyer in the hand or a notice by the time clock does not need a login.

offline.label: It reaches members who skip social media
offline.content: Many members mute work-adjacent groups, never joined the local page, or do not use Facebook or Instagram at all. Print still finds them on the floor.

presence.label: It is a physical reminder the union is here
presence.content: A posted notice is hard to swipe away. It tells everyone walking past that this local is present in the workplace, not only online.

when.tip: If the message matters and the room is mixed — different shifts, languages, or comfort with phones — print it. Flyers for rallies and walkabouts; board notices for ongoing visibility.

flyers.title: Flyers and handouts
flyers.intro: Use Flyer Maker for picket lines, rallies, membership meetings, and walkabouts, then export a PDF for letter, half-letter, or tabloid printing. The tool carries your Brand Kit colours and local number so the stack looks like you.

glance.label: Glance Test
glance.content: Can a member understand the main point in three seconds, from arm's length? If not, enlarge the headline or cut copy until they can.

words.label: Keep the word count low
words.content: Aim for a short headline, a few lines of body, and the facts (what, when, where). If you need a paragraph, the flyer is doing a newsletter's job. Cut it.

action.label: One clear call to action
action.content: Ask for one next step: show up, scan the code, talk to a steward, or share with a coworker. Two asks on one flyer means neither gets done.

qr.label: QR codes bridge print and digital
qr.content: Point the code at your local website, a membership form, or an Officer Hub RSVP link. Paper gives the facts; the scan gives the live page if details change.

type.label: Large, high-contrast type
type.content: Hallways, parking lots, and picket lines are not desks. Keep the text large and dark on a light field (or the reverse) so it still reads outdoors.

flyers.tip: Print one proof and do the Glance Test in a hallway, not at your desk. Test every QR on a phone before you print a stack.

boards.title: Board notices
boards.intro: Use Board Notice Maker for workplace corks. Tabloid (11×17) reads from farther away. Letter (8.5×11) fits most standard boards. Pair this page with the Union Boards Guide for layout, zones, and what to keep up year-round.

place.label: Put boards where members already stop
place.content: Break rooms, time clocks, and the entrance people actually use beat a quiet corridor. If you have more than one site, give each site a board you can keep current.

expired.label: Take down expired notices
expired.content: A meeting flyer still up a week later makes the union look asleep. Pull it the day after, and keep standing pieces (contacts, health and safety, how to find you) current.

agreement.label: Check your collective agreement
agreement.content: Employer rules for union boards live in your collective agreement and any posting policy. Some workplaces only allow union materials on designated boards.

boards.warning: Do not tape a flyer to a door, window, or management board unless your collective agreement or a written posting practice allows it. When you are unsure, ask your president or steward before you post.

logistics.title: Printing logistics and tips
logistics.intro: Most locals print on a tight budget, often on a workplace copier. Design for the machine you actually have, then spend colour money only when the run is official.

bw.label: Design for black and white
bw.content: Colour ink is expensive, and many shop copiers only do greyscale. If the flyer still reads without colour, it will also read in colour — and it will survive a cheap copy.

contrast.label: Keep text contrast high
contrast.content: Pale grey on white fails on a tired copier and in a dim hallway. Dark text on a light field (or the reverse) is the difference between a notice people read and one they walk past.

union.label: Use a unionized print shop when the run is big
union.content: Home and copy-shop letter printing is fine for a meeting stack. For bulk runs or official campaign printing, prefer a unionized print shop when one is available.

proof.label: Print one proof first
proof.content: Letter (8.5×11) is the cheapest stack; tabloid (11×17) is worth it for boards that must read from across a room. Read the proof at arm's length in hallway light before you copy fifty.

logistics.tip: Recycled or slightly heavier stock lasts longer on a cork board than thin copier paper. Save the heavier sheet for standing notices; use cheap letter paper for handouts that will be thrown out after the event.

digital.title: Print plus digital
digital.intro: Print and digital are not competing channels. The same facts should appear on the board, the flyer, social, and the website: one message, four channels.

facts.label: Lock the facts once
facts.content: Date, time, place, and who to contact must match everywhere. If one channel is wrong, members will trust none of them.

order.label: Post paper first when you can
order.content: Hand the flyer or pin the notice, then share a photo of the printed piece on social (with photo consent for anyone visible). Members who only see the feed still see the union on the wall.

qr.label: Let print send people digital
qr.content: A QR code on the flyer or board can open the live page, the RSVP, or the membership form when details change after you print.

digital.tip: If you only have time for one printed piece, make it the board notice or the flyer — then reuse the same headline in Graphic Maker so social does not invent a second message.

emailBroadcastGuide.title: Email & Member Outreach Guide
emailBroadcastGuide.subtitle: Write the official meeting or vote note here, then send it from your inbox.
emailBroadcastGuide.intro: Email is the official record: date, time, place, and the vote link. Social posts are for speed and photos; this page is how you write mail members will actually read. Always use BCC for member lists — never paste addresses in the To field.

when.title: When email fits
when.intro: Email is the anchor of digital communications. Put the final, official details here so they still hold if a social post disappears.

meeting.label: Meeting notices
meeting.content: Send the date, time, and place in mail members already trust, not only in a Facebook post.

rsvp.label: RSVPs and reminders
rsvp.content: Ask people to reply or open a link. A reminder in the inbox is easier to find than a story that vanished overnight.

vote.label: Votes and ratification
vote.content: Put the voting link and the deadline in the first line. Members should not hunt through a thread for the mandate.

bargaining.label: Bargaining updates
bargaining.content: Use email for the update members must be able to find later. Use social for a photo from the table or the picket. Walk the full survey-to-signing path in the Bargaining Lifecycle guide.

when.tip: A social post can carry a photo from the meeting. Email carries the minutes, the vote link, and the time. Do both, and keep the facts the same.

anatomy.title: Write an email members will read
anatomy.intro: Officers skim. Members skim faster. Put the facts first and ask for one action.

subject.label: Subject line
subject.content: Keep it short and specific. "ACTION REQUIRED: Ratification vote Thursday" gets opened. "Local newsletter Q3" does not.

facts.label: Lead with the facts
facts.content: Date, time, location, or the vote link belongs in the first sentence. Do not bury it under three paragraphs of history.

ask.label: One ask
ask.content: Tell members exactly what to do: reply to RSVP, open the mandate, or bring a steward. One email, one action.

local.label: Name the local
local.content: Put the local number in the body so the message is recognizable if it is forwarded.

protect.title: Protect member addresses
protect.intro: A membership list is personal information. Treat every send as if a member's neighbour or employer might see the message.
protect.bccTitle: Use BCC from a personal inbox
protect.bccBody: When you email a list from Outlook or Gmail, put every member in BCC (blind carbon copy). To and CC show every address to every recipient. BCC keeps those addresses private.
protect.employerBody: Never send union business to an address the employer provides. The employer can read that inbox. Collect and use personal email addresses.
protect.cases: Keep grievance files, medical details, and other case notes out of any open broadcast. Those belong in a private channel with the member, not in a local-wide mail.

toolkit.title: Write here, send from your inbox
toolkit.intro: UnionOps is a toolkit, not an email server. You write the content here. You keep the list. You hit send from an inbox you already trust.
toolkit.tools: Document Generator, Board Notice, Graphic Maker, and Flyer Maker include a copy-only invite step. Paste that text into Outlook, Gmail, or the mass-email tool your union already approved.
toolkit.privacyBody: UnionOps does not store member marketing lists, send automatic broadcasts, or handle dues or card payments. For a newsletter, use your union's approved mass-email provider and export graphics from Comms separately.
toolkit.hubTitle: Officer Hub is a separate draft
toolkit.hubBody: Officer Hub can draft a membership-meeting reminder for officers. That is not mass mail from this site, and it is separate from the public invite builders.

checklist.title: Before you hit send
checklist.intro: Work through these once per mail, the same way First week walks boards then print then socials.

items.subject: The subject line names the action and the day, not a generic newsletter.
items.facts: The first sentence has the date, time, place, or vote link.
items.local: The local number is in the body.
items.bcc: Members are in BCC, or you are using the union's approved mass-email tool.
items.personal: You are sending to personal addresses, not employer inboxes.
items.rsvp: A link or QR code is in the mail if people need to RSVP or vote.
items.cases: Sensitive case details are not in this broadcast.

shortFormGuide.title: Short-form Video Guide
shortFormGuide.subtitle: Film on a phone, keep member privacy, and send people to a real ask.
shortFormGuide.intro: UnionOps makes stills and captions. The camera and a phone editor make the clip. Use this page after Brand Kit and a social graphic, not instead of boards, print, or a closed Facebook group.

aspect.caption: Reels, Stories, and Shorts are tall. Graphic Maker is square or landscape today; crop a cover to Instagram Story size in Image Resizer, or export a 9:16 digital Solidarity Poster.

filming.title: Filming on a phone
filming.content: Hold the phone upright for Reels, Stories, and Shorts. Face a window, not a ceiling light. Speak close to the mic, or record a voiceover later in a quiet room. Shop floors and picket lines are loud; a short clip with on-screen text often beats a long take.

items.vertical: Film tall unless you know the post is a Facebook landscape.
items.light: Put faces toward a window or open shade. Avoid backlight that turns a speaker into a silhouette.
items.audio: If the floor is noisy, shoot silent footage and add a voiceover. Do not shout over machines.
items.background: Check who is behind the speaker. Faces, badges, and lanyards identify people too.
items.consent: Do not film grievances, medical spaces, or papers on a desk. Run Photo Consent before any member is on camera.

filming.consentTitle: Privacy is the same checklist as photos
filming.consentBody: Video is harder to crop after the fact. Get consent before you press record, including people clearly visible in the background.

editing.title: Edit on the phone you already have
editing.content: Trim, captions on screen, and a voiceover belong in a phone editor. UnionOps does not edit video. Start with the camera app. Named apps below are common; none of them run inside this site, and some upload footage to a cloud.
editing.stillsBody: Download a 9:16 cover or end card from Graphic Maker (Portrait) or Image Resizer (Instagram Story is 1080×1920), then drop it on the first and last frames. Copy a caption from the library. Point a QR or link at an Action Card, meeting notice, or your local website.

strategy.title: One ask, then a place to go
strategy.content: Open with who, what, and when in the first second. One action per clip. Start with the platform members already use. Many locals still live in a closed Facebook group. TikTok is optional, not a First week step. Skip weekly ranking tips; they go stale. Official how-to pages are in Sources below.

items.hook: Put the ask on screen as well as in speech, so the clip works with the sound off.
items.oneAsk: One meeting, one petition, or one website. Not all three.
items.handoff: Send people to something you already made: a QR, an Action Card, Captions plus Graphic Maker, or the Website Template.
items.platform: Do well on one channel before you split time across Instagram, YouTube Shorts, and TikTok.

checklist.title: Before you post
checklist.intro: Work through these once per clip, the same way First week walks boards then print then socials.

items.consent: Photo Consent is done, including background faces and location tags turned off.
items.cover: A tall cover or end card is exported (Graphic Maker Portrait, Image Resizer Story size, or a 9:16 Solidarity Poster).
items.caption: A caption is copied from the library and edited for this ask. Hashtags stay generic, without a union name.
items.alt: Alt text is drafted in Alt-Text Assistant for the cover still, then pasted into the platform field.
items.ask: The clip points at one action members can take this week.

privacy.on-device: Stays on the phone unless you export
privacy.account-cloud: Needs an account; files may upload
privacy.high-risk-cloud: Cloud account; treat member footage as leaving the phone

device-native.name: Phone camera editor
device-native.when: Trim and titles without a new account. Prefer this when member footage should stay on the device.

inshot.name: InShot
inshot.when: Common for on-screen captions and simple cuts. Check whether a clip uploads before you sign in.

canva.name: Canva
canva.when: Handy if the local already uses Canva for stills. Video and photos go to a cloud account; skip confidential casework.

descript.name: Descript
descript.when: Uploads audio to make a transcript. Do not send grievance, medical, or bargaining talk.

capcut.name: CapCut
capcut.when: Widely used, and a cloud login. Do not treat it as the UnionOps default. Keep member faces and workplace audio off that account when you can.

photoConsentGuide.title: Photo Consent & Member Media
photoConsentGuide.subtitle: Ask before you post — scripts, logs, and takedowns for stewards and comms volunteers
photoConsentGuide.intro: Graphic Maker blocks upload until you acknowledge consent — but locals still need a shared practice for phone cameras, Reels, board photos, and Facebook posts. This playbook helps officers agree on how to ask, what to record, and who takes images down. Not legal advice.

disclaimer.title: Not legal advice
disclaimer.body: Privacy law and collective agreement posting rules vary. Confirm with your local executive and servicing rep before you film in the workplace.

gate.title: Before you raise the camera
gate.intro: Not every union moment needs a face online. Run this gate before you shoot or export.

crowd.label: Wide crowd, no single subject
crowd.content: Picket lines and rallies: backs and signs often suffice. Still avoid tagging individuals or geotagging the gate.

spotlight.label: One member is the story
spotlight.content: Spotlight graphics, quote cards with a face, and Reels need explicit consent and the checklist below.

workplace.label: Filming inside the workplace
workplace.content: Check CA and employer policy first. Probationary and precarious workers face real retaliation risk — default to no unless the member initiates.

crisis.label: Strike or discipline context
crisis.content: Extra caution. A solidarity photo can become evidence management uses. Read the Strike Guide consent lines before you post.

gate.warning: Crop to hands, signs, or wide shots. A missed moment beats harming a member.

why.title: Why consent is solidarity
why.intro: Consent protects members from employer watch and from each other’s good intentions.
why.retaliationBody: Do not tag members at work, leave location on, or post proof they attended a union event if that could be used against them. When in doubt, crop or do not post.

tiers.title: Match the ask to the room
tiers.intro: The same photo rules are not the same in every space.

rally.label: Public rallies and picket lines
rally.content: Wide shots when no one person is the subject. Verbal yes before a close-up. Tell people you may post to the local page.

meeting.label: Closed meetings and internal events
meeting.content: Announce at the start that photos may be taken. Point to a no-photo zone. Honour opt-outs without debate.

workplace.label: High-risk workplaces and small shops
workplace.content: Explicit yes from each identifiable person before you post. Small groups are easy for management to recognize.

tiers.tip: Say where the photo will go — Facebook group, website, board PDF — not just “is it okay if I take one?”

askScript.title: What to say out loud
askScript.intro: Short, direct asks work better than forms nobody reads.

spotlight.label: Member spotlight
spotlight.content: “We would like to feature you on the local Facebook page and maybe the website. You can say no or ask us to take it down anytime. Is that okay?”

meeting.label: Start of meeting
meeting.content: “Photos may be taken for the local page. If you do not want to be in frame, sit in the no-photo corner or tell any officer.”

group.label: Group photo
group.content: “Everyone in frame — we are posting this to the member group. Anyone need to step out?” Wait for heads to nod.

video.label: Reels and Shorts
video.content: Same ask, plus: “This may include your voice and face on Instagram or YouTube.” Point to the short-form video guide for filming basics.

recordKeeping.title: Record consent locally
recordKeeping.intro: You do not need a database. You need a paper trail when someone asks who approved a post.

who.label: Who consented
who.content: Name (or member ID if your local uses numbers), date, and which officer asked.

where.label: Where it will appear
where.content: Facebook, website, board PDF, Reel — list channels. Update the log if you cross-post later.

how.label: Verbal or written
how.content: Text or email counts. Note “verbal yes at membership meeting” if that is what happened.

storage.label: Keep logs with officers
storage.content: Spreadsheet or notebook in union custody — not on employer systems or public Google accounts tied to work email.

recordKeeping.tip: Graphic Maker’s consent step is your reminder at export time — the log is your proof if a member asks later.

checklist.title: Before you post
checklist.intro: Confirm each item before using a member photo in graphics, flyers, board notices, or social posts.

consent.label: Consent captured
consent.content: Written or verbal yes from the member — logged with date and officer name.

public.label: Audience clear
public.content: The member knows which channels will see the image and that they can withdraw consent.

confidential.label: No confidential context
confidential.content: Caption and background free of grievance details, medical info, or bargaining leaks.

group.label: Group photo sweep
group.content: Everyone identifiable is covered — or crop, blur, or pick another image.

minors.label: Minors and dependents
minors.content: Follow local executive and union policy before you publish.

background.label: Background check
background.content: Badges, lanyards, and faces behind the subject count. Crop or wait.

location.label: Location off
location.content: Strip geotags before publish. Do not film confidential casework or medical spaces.

withdrawal.label: Takedown officer named
withdrawal.content: Members know who to text for removal — see below.

takedown.title: If a member asks to come down
takedown.rule: Remove the photo from every channel the same day — social, website, board PDF if you can reprint. No debate, no delay.
takedown.who: Name one officer and a backup in your local practice doc so requests do not bounce.

speed.label: Same day
speed.content: Delete or replace the post. Archive exports on officers’ devices if needed — do not leave old graphics in the group photo album.

everywhere.label: Every copy
everywhere.content: Facebook, Instagram, website hero, printed board — check each place you cross-posted.

log.label: Note the withdrawal
log.content: Update the consent log so volunteers do not repost the same image next month.

thanks.label: Thank the member
thanks.content: “Done — thanks for telling us.” No guilt trip.

privacy.title: Privacy and employer watch
privacy.intro: Member faces are personal information. Consent must be informed.

ipc.label: IPC Ontario
ipc.content: Video and photo capture in workplaces should follow proportionality and notice principles — see sources below.

pipeda.label: PIPEDA baseline
pipeda.content: When employers or vendors collect images, consent must be meaningful — union practice should be at least as careful.

ca.label: Collective agreement
ca.content: Posting and filming rules may live in your CA or employer policy. Stewards check before filming on employer property.

crisis.label: Strike and discipline
crisis.content: Extra risk during crises. Pair with the Strike Guide — solidarity photos are not worth a member’s job.

fullScenario.title: Worked walk-through: member spotlight graphic
fullScenario.intro: A steward wants to celebrate a member who spoke at a rally. You will post a Graphic Maker portrait to the closed Facebook group and the local website.

ask.label: Before the event
ask.content: Steward uses the spotlight script. Member agrees to Facebook and website. Officer logs name, date, and channels in the consent notebook.

shoot.label: At the rally
shoot.content: Wide shots during speeches. After, take the portrait away from employer logos. Member reviews the frame on the phone.

export.label: In Graphic Maker
export.content: Upload photo — complete the consent dialog. Export PNG. Second officer reads caption for confidential details.

post.label: Publish
post.content: Post to group with alt text. Upload to website news section. No location tag.

later.label: If they ask to remove
later.content: Comms officer deletes both posts before end of day, updates log, confirms by text.

fullScenario.tip: Two officers checking beats one enthusiastic poster working alone.

workshop.title: Facilitator note
workshop.intro: In lunch-and-learns, practice the ask script and the Graphic Maker consent dialog together.
workshop.content: Pause on the consent step, walk the checklist once, assign takedown officers, and link Comms Resources plus Privacy. Same rules apply before filming a Reel — see the short-form video guide.

tools.title: Tools and related guides
tools.intro: Consent is built into export paths — use them.

graphic.label: Graphic Maker
graphic.content: Consent gate on member photo upload before export.

shortForm.label: Short-form video guide
shortForm.content: Filming and privacy for Reels and Shorts.

crisis.label: Strike Guide
crisis.content: Consent rules when the local is under pressure.

privacy.label: Privacy page
privacy.content: How Comms data stays on-device and who controls Hub data.

websiteGuide.title: Local Website Guide
websiteGuide.subtitle: Write a simple local site, download a ZIP, then put it online. A volunteer can do the tech steps.
websiteGuide.intro: Boards and socials move messages. A website holds who you are, who to email, and how to find you. Start with Part 1. Stop when the ZIP is on your computer.

glance.title: At a glance
glance.intro: Most locals only need Part 1. Stop when the ZIP is on your computer. Part 2 is for whoever will put those files on the internet.

part1.title: Write and download
part1.body: Gather a few facts, fill Website Template, and download the ZIP. No hosting account yet.

part2.title: Put it online
part2.body: Upload the ZIP to GitHub Pages for free. Skip this if a tech-savvy volunteer will do it.

part1.title: Planning and creating your site
part1.intro: Your job here is to write the content and download a ZIP. You can stop as soon as that file is on your computer.

part2.title: Publishing your site (the tech steps)
part2.intro: These steps put your downloaded ZIP on the internet so members can open a real web address.
part2.handoffTitle: Hand this off if you want
part2.handoff: Now that you have your website ZIP file, it needs to be put on the internet. If you are not comfortable with technical web setup, you can hand your downloaded ZIP file and this guide to a tech-savvy volunteer.

wordpress.title: Already on WordPress?
wordpress.body: Website Template can also download a WordPress theme. UnionOps does not support WordPress. Use that file only if someone already runs your site. Everyone else should stay with the GitHub Pages ZIP in this part.

squarespace.title: On Squarespace?
squarespace.body: Squarespace does not let you install a custom theme from a file. UnionOps cannot export a Squarespace template. If you already pay for Squarespace, rebuild the same sections in their editor using your colours, logo, and copy.

terms.title: A few words you will see

repository.meaning: An online folder on GitHub that holds your site files.

commit.meaning: Save the files you just uploaded, so GitHub keeps them.

deploy.meaning: Turn the site on so the public address starts working.

why.title: Why a local website
why.intro: A local website is not a news feed. It is the page members, media, and new hires still find months later.
why.tip: One clear web address beats a pile of outdated Docs and posts. Put it on boards, QR cards, signatures, and event graphics.

stable.label: A link that stays put
stable.content: Social feeds change and posts scroll away. A website keeps the contact email, officer names, and meeting basics in one place.

search.label: Search and credibility
search.content: Members, media, and employers search for your local. A simple public page beats a sparse Facebook profile alone.

control.label: Your copy, your timeline
control.content: You decide what stays live. No algorithm. The template opens the member’s email app so messages go straight to your inbox.

bareMinimum.title: Bare-minimum local site
bareMinimum.intro: A new member should answer these in under a minute: Who are you? Who runs the local? How do I reach you? Where do I follow updates?

about.title: About your local
about.content: Two short paragraphs: who you represent, where you work, and what you stand for. Orientation, not a novel.

officers.title: Executive officers
officers.content: Names and roles (president, steward coordinator, treasurer). Keep them in Org Chart, then use those names in Website Template after every election.

contact.title: Contact path
contact.content: One monitored local email, plus office address or steward hours if you have them. Prefer one inbox over five personal addresses that go stale.

social.title: Social or member channel
social.content: Link your Facebook group or other member channel. The site points there; social can point back for officers and email.

include.title: What belongs — and what does not
include.intro: Think in layers: always-on identity, campaign updates when active, and a short list of things that belong elsewhere.

always.label: Always on the site
always.content: About text, current officers, contact email, and your main social or group link.

whenActive.label: Add during active rounds
whenActive.content: A short bargaining or strike update paragraph, plus links to official parent-union resources. Not blow-by-blow chat logs.

optional.label: Optional later
optional.content: Meeting calendar, how to file a grievance overview, or links to CA highlights — only if someone will keep them current.

skip.label: Keep off the public site
skip.content: Member personal data, confidential strategy, unconsented photos, and anything your executive has not approved for public posting.

before.title: Before you open the template
before.intro: Five minutes of prep saves a broken-looking site. Gather these from Brand Kit and your local executive.
before.tip: When the site is live, save that web address in Brand Kit. QR cards and board posters can reuse it without retyping.

items.brand: Brand Kit set: local number, colours, and logo. The template picks those up automatically.
items.email: A monitored contact email the local actually checks.
items.officers: Current officer names and roles approved for the public site. Org Chart can fill Website Template.
items.facebook: Facebook group address, or leave the field blank until you have one.

build.title: Build with Website Template
build.intro: Website Template fills a simple site in your browser. Preview it, then download a ZIP. You do not need a hosting account until someone publishes.
build.done: You can stop here. The ZIP on your computer is the file a volunteer needs to put the site online. Part 2 is next only if you are doing that yourself.

open.title: Open Website Template
open.content: Confirm Brand Kit colours and logo look right in the live preview before you type anything else.

fill.title: Fill the fields
fill.content: Add the name, tagline, about text, contact, Facebook, address, and officers. Replace every sample line before anyone publishes.

preview.title: Check the preview
preview.content: Read it like a new member: can you find who to email and who the president is without scrolling forever?

download.title: Download the ZIP
download.content: Save the ZIP to your computer. It holds the site pages, a short README with the same publish steps, and a CNAME.example file if you later add a custom domain.

deploy.title: Publish on GitHub Pages (free)
deploy.intro: GitHub Pages puts a simple site on the internet for free. You need a free GitHub account and about fifteen minutes the first time. The README inside the ZIP repeats these steps.
deploy.tip: The live address usually looks like https://yourusername.github.io/local243-site/. A GitHub organization can give a shorter address later. Either path works.
deploy.docsLead: If a GitHub screen looks different from this guide, use GitHub’s own help:

account.title: Create a free GitHub account
account.content: Sign up at github.com with an email the local can keep. Prefer a shared officer account over one personal login.

repo.title: Create a public repository (an online folder)
repo.content: Click New repository. Name it something clear, for example local243-site. Make it public so free GitHub Pages works. Skip adding a README if you will upload the ZIP next.

upload.title: Upload the ZIP contents, then commit (save)
upload.content: Unzip the file on your computer. Upload index.html, css/, js/, assets/, and README.md to the root of the online folder, not inside an extra folder. Click Commit changes to save the upload.

pages.title: Turn the site on in Settings → Pages
pages.content: Open Settings → Pages. Under Source, choose Deploy from a branch. Select main (or master) and / (root), then Save. That is the deploy step: GitHub starts building the public site.

wait.title: Wait for the live address
wait.content: GitHub usually finishes in a few minutes. Check Settings → Pages for the address, then open it in a private window to confirm links and the contact email.

domain.title: Optional: custom domain for advanced users
domain.intro: Skip this unless you already own a short domain (for example local243.org) and someone can change the address book at the company that sold it. The free github.io address works fine on boards and QR cards.
domain.tip: The ZIP includes a file called CNAME.example. Rename it to CNAME with no file extension, and put only your domain on the first line before you change DNS.
domain.docsLead: GitHub’s step-by-step for pointing a bought domain at Pages:

cname.title: Add a CNAME file (a one-line domain name)
cname.content: In the repository root (the online folder), add a file named CNAME with no file extension. Put only your domain on the first line, for example local243.org. Commit (save) it.

dns.title: Point the domain at GitHub (DNS)
dns.content: At the company where you bought the domain, add the records GitHub lists in its custom-domain help. DNS is the internet’s address book; changes can take minutes to a day.

enable.title: Enter the domain in Settings → Pages
enable.content: In Settings → Pages, type the custom domain, save, and wait until the secure lock (HTTPS) shows as ready. Then save the final address in Brand Kit.

maintain.title: Keep the site current
maintain.intro: A stale officer list is worse than no site. Assign ownership and a light refresh rhythm.

who.title: Who owns it
who.content: Name one site steward. Share the GitHub login or add a second trusted account so updates do not die when someone leaves.

when.title: When to update
when.content: After elections, contact changes, bargaining starts, or when a campaign needs a short public note.

how.title: How to edit
how.content: Easiest: import the site file from last year’s ZIP in Website Template, edit, and upload a fresh ZIP. Or edit index.html in GitHub’s web editor for small fixes.

archive.title: What to remove
archive.content: Delete expired campaign blurbs and old meeting dates. Linking to a year-old “urgent” update teaches members to ignore the site.

pair.title: Pair the site with other channels
pair.intro: The website is the fourth First week channel, not a replacement for boards, print, or social.

boards.label: Union boards
boards.content: Put a site QR in the socials zone of the bare-minimum board so offline members still reach officers.

qr.label: QR link cards
qr.content: Print wallet or letter cards to the live address. Save the website link in Brand Kit first so tools can pull it.

social.label: Social posts
social.content: In bios and pinned posts, link the site for who you are and how to contact. Social for timely updates; site for stable facts.

brand.label: Brand Kit
brand.content: Keep colours and the website address in Brand Kit so regenerating the template or printing new QR materials stays consistent.

purpose.title: What UnionOps Comms is for
purpose.body: Every local needs clear communications on four channels: social media, print, workplace boards, and a simple website.

membershipSignupGuide.title: Membership signup playbook
membershipSignupGuide.subtitle: Build density with real conversations, safe records, and scan-to-sign materials
membershipSignupGuide.intro: Coverage under a CA is not the same as a signed member. This playbook walks stewards from the first conversation through safe record-keeping and welcome materials.

why.title: Why signed membership matters
why.intro: Member signup is not paperwork for its own sake. Every signed card strengthens the local's bargaining power, voting quorum, and ability to reach workers who rarely share a hallway.

density.label: Density is power
density.content: Employers notice when a majority of workers are signed members in good standing. Higher density gives your bargaining team a stronger mandate at the table.

vote.label: Voting rights
vote.content: Many locals require signed membership before a worker can vote on strikes, ratification, or executive elections. An unsigned coworker may be covered by the CA but locked out of those decisions.

bargain.label: Bargaining strength
bargain.content: National and regional staff track membership numbers when they allocate resources to a local. Accurate signed counts help your local get attention during bargaining and disputes.

comms.label: Member-only communication
comms.content: Signed members can be added to private broadcast lists, steward networks, and meeting notices. That reach does not extend to coworkers who are only CA-covered.

conversation.title: The 1-on-1 conversation
conversation.intro: The best signups happen in a short, respectful conversation — not a lecture in the break room. Use this four-step frame on the shop floor or over coffee.

listen.label: Listen first
listen.content: Ask what is frustrating them at work right now. Pay attention to scheduling, workload, safety, favouritism, or pay — whatever they raise first.

connect.label: Connect the issue to collective action
connect.content: Explain that the problem they named is exactly what a union solves together. One person complaining alone rarely moves management; a organized local does.

explain.label: Explain what the union does
explain.content: Keep it concrete: stewards, grievances, bargaining, training, and solidarity when someone is disciplined or laid off. Avoid abstract slogans.

ask.label: Ask directly
ask.content: Hand them a card or point to the QR and say: "Will you sign up today?" A clear ask beats hoping they find the form on their own.

paper.title: Paper signup workflow
paper.intro: Many locals still use physical membership cards or paper application forms. Treat every completed card like confidential personal information from the moment it is signed.

legible.label: Check legibility on the spot
legible.content: Confirm name, employee ID, personal phone, and personal email are readable before the coworker walks away. Illegible cards delay processing at the union office.

handoff.label: Same-day handoff
handoff.content: Deliver completed cards to your secretary-treasurer or membership officer the same shift when possible. Do not leave a stack in a shared steward locker overnight.

storage.label: Secure local storage
storage.content: Keep blank and completed cards in a locked drawer or cabinet the employer does not control — union office, steward's personal bag, or a local-only storage space.

processing.label: Confirm receipt
processing.content: Ask the membership officer to acknowledge when cards are logged. New members should know their signup reached the right person.

digital.title: Digital and scan-to-sign workflow
digital.intro: QR posters and online forms reach part-time and remote workers who never pass a union board. Point every QR to a form your national or local union hosts — not a spreadsheet on a work account.

urls.label: Use your union's official form
urls.content: Paste the membership URL your national or local union approved into Brand Kit. If your local has separate collections, add one link per group.

qr.label: Put QR where people pause
qr.content: Boards, break rooms, and event tables work best. A pocket QR card lets stewards start the conversation and hand over a scannable link in the same breath.

test.label: Test before you print
test.content: Scan every QR on your own phone before you print a stack. Confirm it opens the correct form for the right collection.

collection.label: Match the collection
collection.content: Full-time and part-time groups often have different signup URLs. Label each QR clearly so a worker lands on the form meant for their job class.

digital.testTip: If a QR fails on your phone, it will fail for every coworker. Fix the link in Brand Kit before you reprint.

privacy.title: Protect member data
privacy.intro: A membership list is personal information. Treat every signup card, spreadsheet, and contact list as if management could see it — because on employer systems, they often can.
privacy.employerDriveBody: Do not store completed membership cards, signup spreadsheets, or contact lists on Google Drive, OneDrive, or SharePoint tied to a work email. Your employer can access those accounts. Use a personal device, a union-only account, or paper locked at the local.
privacy.personalContactBody: Ask for a personal email address and personal phone number — not the employer-provided inbox or extension. Management can read work email and monitor work phones.
privacy.cases: UnionOps Comms tools stay on your device and do not store member lists. For broadcast email after signup, follow the privacy steps in the Email & outreach guide.

materials.intro: Once your membership URLs are in Brand Kit, these three UnionOps steps produce matching posters, cards, and a welcome letter — all pulling from the same links.

brandKit.body: Paste membership form URLs in Brand Kit — one link or separate links per collection. Every QR tool and the welcome letter reuse them automatically.

printMaterials.body: Print a QR Board poster for the break room, pocket QR cards for stewards, and a Solidarity Poster with a clear signup ask. Use collection-specific presets when your local has more than one group.

welcome.body: Document Generator welcome letter pulls your membership URL and collection from Brand Kit. Hand it to new members the same day they sign.

onboarding.title: Next steps after someone signs
onboarding.intro: A signature is the start, not the finish. These steps turn a new signup into an active member who knows how to reach the local.

welcome.label: Send a welcome
welcome.content: Hand them a printed welcome letter or email the text from Document Generator. Include the steward contact, next meeting date, and how to finish any remaining application steps.

steward.label: Introduce their steward
steward.content: Give them a steward name, phone number, or QR card for local support. New members should know who to call before a problem becomes a crisis.

broadcast.label: Add to the member list
broadcast.content: Add their personal email to the local's private broadcast list — using BCC, never employer email. See the Email & outreach guide for safe sending.

confirm.label: Confirm with the membership officer
confirm.content: Check that the card or online form reached the secretary-treasurer and was logged. Follow up if the worker asks whether they are in good standing.

crisisGuide.title: Strike & Crisis Comms Guide
crisisGuide.subtitle: One voice, three messages a day, and a channel plan when the local is under pressure
crisisGuide.intro: Crisis comms is not “post more.” It is who may speak, what members need to hear, and what never goes on a public channel. Locals handle day-to-day messaging; your provincial or national union supports sector bargaining — but the Facebook group still needs one local voice.

disclaimer.body: Nothing in this guide replaces your local executive or servicing rep. When in doubt, draft offline and wait for president approval before you publish.

gate.title: Before you post — is this crisis comms?
gate.intro: Normal comms can be steward-led. Crisis comms needs a short chain of command so members are not reading five conflicting voices.

strike.label: Strike or lockout live
strike.content: Use this guide. One comms lead, one spokesperson, president approves every public post.

bargaining.label: Bargaining countdown
bargaining.content: Use the bargaining section and the three-messages rule. Share only what the bargaining team cleared for release.

layoff.label: Layoffs or restructuring announced
layoff.content: Calm, factual tone. Point to stewards and EAP. No guessing about who is affected.

normal.label: Routine local update
normal.content: Use The Blueprint and channel guides instead. Crisis rules are heavier than you need for a meeting reminder.

gate.warningTitle: If two officers are posting different facts
gate.warning: Stop public posting until president and comms lead align on one correction. Members trust silence less than they hate contradiction — but contradiction kills trust fastest.

roles.title: Who does what
roles.intro: Write names on a sticky note before the picket line opens. Volunteers rotate; roles do not.

president.label: President
president.content: Final yes on every public post, media callback, and correction. Can delegate drafting, not approval.

comms.label: Comms lead
comms.content: Owns the draft queue, Brand Kit exports, and the website strike page. Does not improvise bargaining facts.

spokesperson.label: Spokesperson
spokesperson.content: One or two people for media and member questions at the gate. Everyone else sends reporters to them.

servicing.label: Servicing rep
servicing.content: Legal and bargaining context. Not usually the daily poster — but clears language about rights and process.

roles.tip: Post the spokesperson phone number on the strike page and one pinned social post — then stop answering bargaining questions in comments.

strike.title: Strike action comms
strike.intro: Members need schedule, safety, and pay questions answered from one place. Management will test whether you fracture in public.

approve.label: President approves every post
approve.content: Draft in Graphic Maker or Flyer Maker, export, then send the PNG/PDF to president before it goes live.

schedule.label: Daily picket schedule
schedule.content: Gate locations, start times, and weather/safety reminders. Board Notice at each gate; same facts on the website.

safety.label: Safety first on the line
safety.content: No member addresses, no dare posts, no live-streaming confrontations. Incident? Follow emergency protocol before you post.

consent.label: Photos with consent
consent.content: Solidarity shots need the Photo Consent checklist. Wide crowd frames beat close-ups when consent is unclear.

sector.label: Follow sector materials when coordinating
sector.content: Use division or national campaign hashtags and graphics when you are aligned — do not invent parallel branding.

questions.label: Pay and return-to-work questions
questions.content: Send to the strike committee or spokesperson — not comment threads. Link the official FAQ when you have one.

bargaining.title: Bargaining countdown comms
bargaining.intro: Build urgency without leaking table language. Members should feel informed, not briefed on confidential proposals.

facts.label: Factual priorities only
facts.content: Job security, workload, wages — in member language. No article numbers or counter-proposal figures unless the team cleared them.

hashtag.label: One visual system
hashtag.content: Same Brand Kit colours and hashtag on every graphic so members recognize official posts instantly.

meetings.label: Meeting times early
meetings.content: Information meetings need two weeks’ notice when you can. Flyer + board + social + website with identical times.

approved.label: Bargaining team clears releases
approved.content: If it did not come from the team, it does not go public — including enthusiastic stewards paraphrasing from memory.

comments.label: Ignore management bait
comments.content: One pinned correction beats twenty angry replies. See management pushback below.

link.label: Link official bargaining pages
link.content: Point to national or divisional bargaining hubs rather than retyping updates that may change overnight.

layoffs.title: Layoffs and restructuring
layoffs.intro: Members are scared. Your job is calm routing to stewards and facts — not speculation about who is on a list.

empathy.label: Acknowledge fear
empathy.content: Short, human posts. “We know this is stressful” beats false certainty.

route.label: Route to stewards and EAP
route.content: Phone numbers and meeting times in one pinned post. Repeat on boards where affected members actually walk.

facts.label: Employer and union facts only
facts.content: Quote confirmed letters and local executive statements. Screenshot management email for the file — do not forward member names publicly.

leaders.label: Unified local voice
leaders.content: Quote Card from president or chief steward. One statement, not five officers venting.

record.label: Document offline
record.content: Save employer comms for consultation and grievance records. Public posts are not the archive.

names.label: No naming individuals
names.content: Unless a member asked to be identified. Layoff fear spreads faster when people see a coworker tagged.

management.title: Management pushback and misinformation
management.intro: Employers post to spook members. You respond once, factually, then return to your schedule.

facts.label: CA language and dates
facts.content: Quote the agreement or the employer’s own letter. No personal attacks on managers.

correction.label: One correction post
correction.content: Brief Quote Card or graphic. Pin it. Do not thread-war with the college account.

harassment.label: Escalate threats immediately
harassment.content: Harassment, surveillance, or legal letters go to president and servicing rep the same hour — not after the shift.

screenshot.label: Screenshot for the file
screenshot.content: Send problematic employer posts to executive offline. Public clapbacks are not evidence.

stewards.label: Member issues stay private
stewards.content: Discipline, medical, and bargaining details belong in steward channels — never in a public reply.

management.warning: Table blow-by-blow feels satisfying and helps management. If it is not on the bargaining team release sheet, it stays offline.

rhythm.title: Three messages a day
rhythm.intro: During strike or late bargaining, members check phones constantly. Give them a predictable rhythm instead of panic posting.

morning.label: Morning — schedule and safety
morning.content: Picket gates, weather, any line protocol change. Board Notice PDF plus one social post.

midday.label: Midday — only if facts changed
midday.content: Skip if nothing new. Silence beats noise when the facts are stable.

evening.label: Evening — recap and tomorrow
evening.content: Thank members, confirm tomorrow’s schedule, link website FAQ. No new bargaining details unless cleared.

queue.label: Draft queue in one doc
queue.content: Comms lead holds drafts; president batch-approves. Prevents duplicate posts from well-meaning volunteers.

rhythm.tip: Write tomorrow’s three messages tonight. Crisis mornings are not for drafting from scratch.

fullScenario.title: Worked walk-through: strike day 3 after a management memo
fullScenario.intro: Management emailed a misleading return-to-work offer at 7 a.m. Picket line opened at 6:30. The Facebook group is spiraling.

t715.label: 7:15 — hold the channel
t715.content: Comms lead posts “Hold for official local update” in the group. Mute notifications on bait comments. President and servicing rep read the memo.

t730.label: 7:30 — one correction
t730.content: Quote Card with three approved bullets. Pin to group. Same text on website strike page. No negotiation analysis.

t800.label: 8:00 — gates
t800.content: Board Notice at each gate: today’s schedule + “Ignore management memo — read pinned post.”

t1000.label: 10:00 — executive sync
t1000.content: Servicing rep joins a 10-minute call. Decide if a second post is needed. Default no unless facts changed.

t1400.label: 14:00 — member story
t1400.content: Graphic Maker spotlight only after written consent. No employer logos in frame.

t1700.label: 17:00 — boards
t1700.content: Pull expired meeting flyers. Leave contacts strip up overnight.

fullScenario.tip: If you posted more than three times before lunch, you probably posted too much.

escalation.title: When to escalate immediately
escalation.intro: Some events skip the draft queue and go straight to president and servicing rep.

media.label: Media calls
media.content: Route to spokesperson. Never “just answer one question” without president aware.

legal.label: Legal threats or injunctions
legal.content: Stop posting. Forward the letter. Wait for legal guidance.

safety.label: Line or workplace safety incident
safety.content: Emergency protocols first. Comms only after members are safe and leadership agrees on facts.

leak.label: Leaked confidential documents
leak.content: Do not share. Alert president and servicing rep. Public speculation helps the employer.

viral.label: Viral misinformation
viral.content: One coordinated correction from the local account. Tell stewards to share the pinned post, not invent their own rebuttal.

tools.title: On-device tools for crisis comms
tools.intro: Keep visuals consistent when volunteers rotate. Everything runs on your device — no ad hoc Canva accounts.

brand.label: Brand Kit
brand.content: Local number, colours, and logo locked before day one of the strike.

board.label: Board Notice Maker
board.content: Tabloid schedule notices for gates and break rooms.

flyer.label: Flyer Maker and Quote Card
flyer.content: Leadership statements and one-page member FAQs.

graphic.label: Graphic Maker
graphic.content: Member spotlights with built-in consent gate.

web.label: Website Template
web.content: One stable URL for media and members — update the strike page, not five different links.

captions.label: Captions library
captions.content: Pre-written solidarity posts you can adapt after president approval.

dfrGuide.title: Duty of Fair Representation playbook
dfrGuide.subtitle: From first member call to a defensible file — statutes, clocks, and plain-language member updates
dfrGuide.intro: Duty of fair representation (DFR) is the union’s legal duty to handle each member’s representation without arbitrariness, discrimination, or bad faith. Most board complaints grow from missed clocks and silence, not malice. This playbook walks stewards through intake, investigation, deadlines, and member conversations across Ontario private sector (LRA), college (CCBA), and federal (CLC) regimes. Orientation only — not legal advice.

disclaimer.title: Not legal advice
disclaimer.body: This page helps stewards run a fair process. It does not coach members to file against the union. Confirm procedure with your local officers and counsel.

gate.title: Before you open a file — who owes what
gate.intro: DFR binds the union, not individual stewards personally — but stewards create the paper trail officers and boards will read. Run this gate on every new member contact.

steward.label: Steward role
steward.content: You intake facts, start the clock, and document what you did. You do not promise outcomes. Hand complex or conflict files to an officer the same day.

member.label: Member rights
member.content: Members can ask how their file is handled and get a written answer if the union declines to grieve. They cannot demand that every complaint become a grievance.

officer.label: Officer decision
officer.content: Local officers (or your CA’s named decision-maker) decide whether to file, advance, or settle. That decision must follow a real investigation — not a hallway vote with no notes.

conflict.label: Conflict of interest
conflict.content: If you cannot represent the member fairly — same department feud, family tie, or you are a witness — recuse in writing and name who took the file.

gate.warning: A thoughtful “no” with a written explanation rarely loses a DFR complaint. Ghosting the member after intake, or missing a CA deadline while deciding, is what boards punish.

scope.title: Which statute and board apply
scope.intro: DFR language is similar across regimes, but the act and board differ. Confirm coverage before you cite a section in a member letter.

ontario.label: Most Ontario private-sector unions
ontario.content: Labour Relations Act, 1995 s.74 — complaints go to the Ontario Labour Relations Board (OLRB). Read Information Bulletin 12 for the member-facing test.

college.label: Ontario college support staff
college.content: Colleges Collective Bargaining Act, 2008 — not the LRA. Confirm your unit’s act with your servicing rep before quoting a section number.

federal.label: Federally regulated workplaces
federal.content: Canada Labour Code s.37 — complaints go to the Canada Industrial Relations Board (CIRB). Same arbitrary / discriminatory / bad faith language, different board and forms.

legalTest.title: The arbitrary / discriminatory / bad faith test
legalTest.intro: Boards and courts look for honesty of purpose, non-discrimination, and a non-arbitrary process. Perfect outcomes are not required — a serious process is.

arbitrary.label: Arbitrary
arbitrary.content: Rubber-stamping a refusal, never reading the file, treating similar cases differently for no documented reason, or missing a known CA deadline without an extension on record.

discriminatory.label: Discriminatory
discriminatory.content: Treating members differently because of protected grounds, local politics, or personal dislike. Apply the same intake and investigation steps to every member.

badFaith.label: Bad faith
badFaith.content: Lying to the member, burying evidence, advancing a personal agenda, or punishing a member for criticizing the local.

honest.label: Honest disagreement
honest.content: After a real investigation, officers may reasonably decline a grievance. Document what you reviewed and why — a member can disagree without that being a DFR breach.

intake.title: Day zero — open the file
intake.intro: The member’s first call sets every clock. Capture facts before opinions, and log the contact before you hang up.

log.label: Same-day log entry
log.content: Record date, member name, contact info, supervisor or manager, what happened, and which CA articles might apply. One paragraph is enough — but it must exist.

calendar.label: Calendar every deadline
calendar.content: Count forward from the triggering event: Step 1 filing, referral to arbitration, policy grievance windows. Put each date in your calendar and Officer Hub if you use it.

member.label: Set expectations
member.content: Tell the member you will investigate before deciding. Do not say “we will win” or “this is definitely a grievance.” Give a realistic return date for your next update.

conflict.label: Hand off conflicts
conflict.content: If you cannot act fairly, email the president or chief steward the same day: member name, issue summary, and who is taking the file. Do not leave the member waiting while you “think about it.”

intake.tip: If you only do one thing: write the intake note before end of shift. Memory is not a file.

investigate.title: Days 1–3 — build the record
investigate.intro: Boards ask what the union did, not what it believed. Neutral notes beat clever arguments.

interview.label: Interview the member
interview.content: Ask what happened, who was present, and what documents exist. Summarize in neutral language — “Member states…” — not “Member is right.”

documents.label: Request employer documents
documents.content: Discipline letters, emails, schedules, attendance records — whatever the CA lets you request. Log the date sent and the date received.

witnesses.label: Identify witnesses
witnesses.content: List names and what each might know. You do not need every statement before officers decide, but you must show you asked.

notes.label: Keep internal notes internal
notes.content: Strategy belongs in the officer file — not group texts, not public social posts, not employer cc lines. Redact before sharing anything with the member.

clocks.title: CA deadlines — count forward
clocks.intro: Missed grievance clocks are the fastest path to a DFR complaint. Your CA defines the trigger; this section is about discipline-style files where the event starts the clock.

trigger.label: Find the triggering event
trigger.content: Usually the date of discipline, the date the member knew about the decision, or the date of the alleged violation — your CA names which. Write that date at the top of the file.

count.label: Count business or calendar days
count.content: Read the CA literally: business days vs calendar days, whether weekends count, and whether the clock runs to the employer or the union. When unsure, ask your servicing rep before the window closes.

extension.label: Extensions in writing
extension.content: If the employer agrees to extend a Step 1 meeting or filing window, get it in email or letter before the original date passes. “They said it was fine on the phone” is not a file.

late.label: If you are already late
late.content: Stop and escalate to an officer immediately. Document when you discovered the miss and what remedy the CA allows — sometimes late filing can still be argued, but only with counsel involved.

clocks.warning: Officer Hub grievance tools track steps and due dates — use them. A sticky note on your monitor does not survive vacation coverage.

decline.title: When the union says no — say it in writing
decline.intro: Declining is lawful when the process was real. Silence or vague verbal brush-offs are what members take to the board.

written.label: Written explanation
written.content: Plain language: what you reviewed (dates, documents, interviews), why the facts do not meet the grievance test under the CA, and the effective decision date.

review.label: Offer a review path
review.content: Name who can reconsider — president, executive board, servicing rep — and how to reach them. Follow your local constitution if it adds steps.

escalate.label: Escalate internally first
escalate.content: If the member asks for review, treat it seriously. A second pair of eyes on the same facts is cheap insurance against a DFR filing.

silence.label: Never ghost
silence.content: Even a short email — “We reviewed your file on [date] and will not file a grievance because…” — closes the loop. No response reads as bad faith.

decline.tip: Members remember tone, but boards read timestamps. Send the letter within a few days of the officer decision.

fullScenario.title: Worked walk-through: written warning intake
fullScenario.intro: Member Alex receives a written warning on Monday, 3 March 2026, for “failure to follow scheduling procedure.” Alex believes the warning is without just cause. Your CA gives ten calendar days from receipt to file Step 1. Step 1 deadline: Thursday, 13 March 2026.

d0.label: Day 0 — Monday 3 March
d0.content: Alex calls at 4 p.m. You log intake: warning letter date, supervisor name, CA discipline article, and Step 1 due 13 March. You calendar 11 March as your internal “officer decision” date to leave two days’ slack.

d2.label: Day 2 — Wednesday 5 March
d2.content: You interview Alex and request the warning letter plus scheduling emails from HR. A colleague witness may confirm the shift was changed after Alex clocked in. Notes go in the file — facts only.

d4.label: Day 4 — Friday 7 March
d4.content: Documents arrive. Officers review: warning cites a procedure Alex was never trained on. Decision: file Step 1. If instead the facts were weak, you would draft the decline letter now — not after the 13th.

d6.label: Day 8 — Tuesday 11 March
d6.content: Step 1 meeting scheduled with employer for 12 March. Alex gets a plain-language update: what was filed, meeting date, and steward attendance. If you had declined, Alex would have the written explanation by today.

fullScenario.tip: Copy this timeline structure for any discipline file — swap dates, keep the spacing between intake, investigation, decision, and member update.

failureModes.title: What loses DFR complaints in practice
failureModes.intro: Most cases are process failures, not evil intent. Leave a paper trail that shows serious consideration.

missedClock.label: Missed Step or referral deadline
missedClock.content: The CA clock expired while the file sat in someone’s inbox. No extension on record. Fix: calendar at intake; escalate the day you see risk.

noFile.label: No investigation on record
noFile.content: No interview notes, document requests, or officer decision memo. Fix: four neutral paragraphs in the file beat a perfect oral argument with nothing written down.

noLetter.label: Verbal no with no follow-up
noLetter.content: Member told “we’re not grieving this” in a parking lot, never gets mail or email. Fix: send the decline template the same week officers decide.

overPromise.label: Promising victory
overPromise.content: “We will get this thrown out” — then a decline lands. Fix: promise process and timelines, not outcomes.

personalBias.label: Personal conflict driving the decision
personalBias.content: Steward dislikes the member or favours the supervisor. Fix: recuse early; let another steward or officer own the file with clean notes.

memberTalk.title: What to say — and not say — to the member
memberTalk.intro: Good member communication prevents DFR complaints as often as good files do. Plain language, realistic timelines, confidentiality.

promise.label: Do not promise outcomes
promise.content: Say: “I will investigate and the executive will decide whether to file.” Not: “This is an open-and-shut grievance” or “HR will back down once they see our letter.”

status.label: Status on a schedule
status.content: If you promise an update by Friday, send one — even if the answer is “still waiting on documents.” Silence reads as abandonment.

confidential.label: Keep their story confidential
confidential.content: Do not discuss the member’s case in the lunch room or on local social channels. Share facts only with officers who need them for the file.

respect.label: Disagreement is allowed
respect.content: A member may be angry when you decline. Stay professional, point to the written explanation, and name the review path. Do not argue in text threads.

hub.body: Officer Hub grievance tools log steps, due dates, and handoffs so coverage stewards see the same clocks you do. They support a fair process — they do not replace legal judgment or your servicing rep.
