whatIsSteward.title: What is a steward?
whatIsSteward.intro: A steward is an elected union representative on the shop floor — not management, not HR, and not a lawyer.

elected.label: Elected by members
elected.content: Stewards are chosen by the bargaining unit they represent. Your authority comes from the members and your CA — not from the employer.

daily.label: Daily face of the union
daily.content: Members come to you first with problems, questions, and fear. You listen, investigate, and connect them to the local executive when the file outgrows one person.

notManagement.label: Not management's partner
notManagement.content: You can be professional without being management's messenger. Your job is to enforce the contract and build member power — not to smooth over violations.

withExecutive.label: Works with the executive
withExecutive.content: Strategy and major decisions sit with the Local Executive and servicing rep. You carry that strategy to the floor and bring member reality back up.

unionBasics.title: Union in 60 seconds
unionBasics.body: Your bargaining unit is the group of workers covered by one Collective Agreement (CA). The union negotiates that CA with the employer and represents members when the employer breaks it. Solidarity — members acting together — is what gives a grievance teeth.

first48Hours.title: Your first 48 hours
first48Hours.intro: You do not need permission to start doing the job well. Run this checklist in your first two days on the role.

introduce.label: Introduce yourself
introduce.content: Tell your coworkers you are the steward, how to reach you, and that conversations are confidential unless they ask you to share.

backup.label: Get a backup
backup.content: Exchange numbers with the chief steward or another steward. Coverage matters when you are on leave or in a meeting yourself.

caArticles.label: Read key CA articles
caArticles.content: Find discipline, grievance procedure, steward rights, and overtime or scheduling — whatever drives complaints in your workplace.

notes.label: Start a notes habit
notes.content: Date, names, facts, and CA articles. Write what happened — not what you think it means. You will need this if the file grows.

first48Hours.tip: If you only do one thing: put your name and contact on the union board so members know who to call.

threeHats.title: The Three Hats of a Steward
threeHats.intro: Effective stewards switch between three roles. Know which hat you are wearing before you act.

enforcer.label: The Enforcer
enforcer.summary: Management will break the contract if they think they can get away with it. Your job is to know the CA better than management and act when it is violated.

bullets.knowCa: Know the articles that govern discipline, scheduling, leave, and pay in your unit.
bullets.investigate: Investigate with the 6 W's before you promise a grievance — see the grievance playbook.
bullets.file: File when the facts and the contract support it — not to vent frustration.

communicator.label: The Communicator
communicator.summary: You are the bridge between the Local Executive and the members.

bullets.down: Carry executive decisions and bargaining updates to the floor in plain language.
bullets.up: Bring member anger, fears, and ideas back to the executive without filtering them out.
bullets.accurate: Do not invent outcomes. Say what you know, what you are checking, and when you will report back.

organizer.label: The Organizer
organizer.summary: A grievance on paper is weak without power behind it. Your job is to build solidarity.

bullets.map: Map who works where and who listens to whom — see the workplace mapping playbook.
bullets.leaders: Identify organic leaders coworkers already trust.
bullets.action: Mobilize coworkers for petitions, turnout, and collective pressure when the file needs it.

whichHat.title: Which hat when?
whichHat.intro: Not every problem is a grievance. Pick the right mode before you act.

desk.label: Desk complaint or question
desk.content: Start as Communicator — listen, clarify facts, check the CA. Enforcer only if the contract is clearly violated.

discipline.label: Discipline or investigatory meeting
discipline.content: Enforcer + Communicator. Request representation, caucus with the member, advise — do not let management rush a confession.

mobilize.label: Group issue or employer stonewalling
mobilize.content: Organizer hat. Map who is affected, find leaders, and bring numbers to the executive before you file alone.

whichHat.warning: Filing without investigation or member support burns credibility with both management and members. Investigate first — then decide with the executive if the file has merit.

representation.title: The Right to Representation
representation.intro: Under almost all collective agreements, workers have the right to union representation during any meeting that could lead to discipline.

trigger.title: When to invoke it
trigger.body: If management calls a member into an office and begins asking investigative questions about conduct, performance, or an incident, treat it as a discipline-risk meeting — even if they call it "just a chat."

script.title: What the member says
script.body: Instruct the member to say: "If this discussion could in any way lead to my being disciplined or terminated, I respectfully request that my union steward be present."

before.label: Before the meeting
before.content: Meet the member privately. Get their timeline of facts, names, and what they think management wants. Remind them they can pause and ask to caucus with you at any time.

during.label: During the meeting
during.content: You are not a silent witness. Ask clarifying questions, object to vague accusations, and request breaks to advise the member. Do not answer for them.

after.label: After the meeting
after.content: Debrief immediately. Write notes while memory is fresh. Decide with the member whether to grieve, and loop in the chief steward if discipline is issued.

denied.title: If management delays or denies your presence
denied.body: Document the date, time, and who refused. The member should repeat the request and not answer substantive questions alone. Escalate to your chief steward the same day — continuing without representation may still be a CA violation.

dfr.title: The Duty of Fair Representation (DFR)
dfr.intro: This is a critical legal obligation. Labour law requires unions to represent all members of the bargaining unit fairly, in good faith, and without discrimination or arbitrary decisions.

items.meaning: What this means: You cannot refuse to file a grievance or represent a member simply because you personally dislike them, or because they voted against the union.
items.investigate: You must thoroughly investigate every complaint objectively. If a grievance lacks merit and the union decides not to proceed, that decision must be based on the facts and the contract, not personal bias.

dfr.linkIntro: For intake clocks, investigation steps, and decline letters, open the full DFR playbook.

scenario.title: Worked example: discipline meeting
scenario.intro: A member texts: "HR called me in tomorrow about the email I sent." Walk it in order.

text.label: Tonight
text.content: Reply: do not discuss the email with management until you meet. Send the member script. Confirm meeting time and location.

prep.label: Before the meeting
prep.content: Private prep: what happened, who saw it, what policy or CA article applies. Agree the member will ask for a break if unsure before answering.

meeting.label: In the room
meeting.content: Management states the allegation. You ask what policy was violated and request specifics. Caucus if they push for an on-the-spot written statement.

after.label: Same day
after.content: Debrief notes to chief steward. If a warning is issued, start the 6 W's and check grievance clocks in the CA.

scenario.tip: Your job in the room is to protect the member's rights — not to win the argument on the spot.

escalate.title: When to escalate
escalate.intro: You are not alone on hard files. Loop in the next level early when any of these apply.

chief.label: Chief steward
chief.content: Discipline issued, representation denied, or a file that crosses departments or shifts you do not cover.

president.label: Local president
president.content: Employer refuses to meet, policy change affecting the whole unit, or media/legal exposure.

rep.label: Servicing representative
rep.content: Arbitration decision, complex legal question, or a DFR-sensitive decline. Bring dated notes, CA citations, and what the member was told.

escalate.warning: Do not drop a messy file on the executive with "what do I do?" Bring facts, dates, witnesses, CA articles, and what you already tried.

stewardChecklist.title: Steward pocket checklist
stewardChecklist.intro: Print this list or save it on your phone. Run it on every new file.

introduce.label: Member knows how to reach you
introduce.content: Your name and contact are on the union board and in the break room.

listen.label: Listen before you promise
listen.content: Get facts first. Do not say "we will win" or "we will file" until you investigate.

script.label: Discipline-risk meeting
script.content: Member knows the representation script before they walk into the room.

notes.label: Notes same day
notes.content: Date, names, CA articles, and what was said — while memory is fresh.

escalate.label: Loop in chief steward
escalate.content: Discipline issued, representation denied, or a file outside your coverage.

dfr.label: Every member, every file
dfr.content: Investigate objectively. Personal dislike is never a reason to refuse representation.

referenceMaterials.title: Print and reference materials
referenceMaterials.intro: Carry these on the floor — pocket cards, intake sheets, and board pieces members can find without asking.

pocketCard.title: Representation pocket card
pocketCard.body: Wallet-size card with the member script and a QR link back to this guide. Export from QR Link Cards.

intakeSheet.title: Steward intake sheet (CSV)
intakeSheet.body: Log the 6 W's on your personal device — not employer email. One row per file.
intakeSheet.hint: Opens in Excel or another spreadsheet app on your own device.

grievanceWorksheet.title: 6 W's worksheet (XLSX)
grievanceWorksheet.body: Branded spreadsheet from Document Generator when a file is ready for formal intake.

board.title: Steward list on the board
board.body: Print an Org Chart or Board Notice so members know who to call before a crisis.

followUp.title: Member follow-up letter
followUp.body: After a meeting, send a short written recap of what you discussed and the next step.

stewardGuides.title: Steward meeting guides
stewardGuides.body: On-device workspaces for complaint vs grievance triage, pre-disciplinary meetings, and return-to-work intake.

hub.title: Track files in Officer Hub
hub.body: When your local uses Officer Hub, grievance tools log steps, due dates, and handoffs so coverage stewards see the same clocks you do.

goldenRule.title: The Golden Rule of Stewarding
goldenRule.body: Never promise a member you will "win" their case. You do not make the final decision — an arbitrator or management does. Promise only that you will fight for them and represent them to the absolute best of your ability.

next.title: Go deeper
next.body: Work through these playbooks in order while you wait for local or national steward training.

grievanceGuide.title: The Steward's Guide to Grievances
grievanceGuide.subtitle: How to open and walk a file — 6 W's, clocks, and your CA's steps
grievanceGuide.intro: A grievance is a formal complaint that the employer violated the Collective Agreement, past practice, or labour law. This playbook is how to open and walk a file: pick the right forum, log facts, count clocks, and hand off a clean record. Your CA names the steps. Duty of fair representation is the other playbook.

disclaimer.title: Not legal advice
disclaimer.body: UnionOps is a tool, not counsel. This playbook helps stewards run a fair file. It does not replace your Collective Agreement, local bylaws, or your servicing representative. Confirm every clock and step name in the agreement you actually work under.

gate.title: Is this a grievance?
gate.intro: Not every workplace problem is a grievance. Pick the forum before you start a clock you cannot stop.

informal.label: Stay informal
informal.content: A one-off mix-up, a question about how a rule works, or something the supervisor can fix today. Log the conversation. Do not file to vent.

grievance.label: Grievance
grievance.content: A named CA article, past practice, or labour law looks broken, a member is harmed, and you can name a remedy. Open a file.

refusal.label: Right to refuse
refusal.content: Imminent danger or a health and safety refusal is an OHSA process, not a grievance form. Use the right-to-refuse playbook, then file a grievance only if the CA or the refusal outcome requires it.

bump.label: Seniority or bumping
bump.content: Displacement, recall, or a bump claim. Use the seniority playbook and the committee worksheet. A grievance may follow if the employer skipped the CA process.

joint.label: Joint table
joint.content: A campus-wide practice that belongs at a union-management committee, not a single-member grievance. Use the joint-committee playbook.

gate.flowCaption: Walk these questions in order before you start a clock.

start.label: Member brings a problem
start.content: Listen first. Do not promise an outcome.

safety.label: Imminent danger or OHSA refusal?
safety.content: Stop. Use the right-to-refuse playbook. File a grievance only if the CA or the refusal outcome requires it.

bump.label: Displacement, recall, or bumping?
bump.content: Use the seniority playbook and worksheet. A grievance may follow if the employer skipped the CA process.

system.label: Campus-wide practice, not one member?
system.content: Use the joint-committee playbook. Do not bury a system issue in a single-member file.

informal.label: Can the supervisor fix it today?
informal.content: Log the conversation. Stay informal. Do not file to vent.

file.label: CA article broken, harm, and a named remedy?
file.content: Open a file. Print the 6 W's worksheet and count the clock.

investigation.title: The 6 W's that teach
investigation.intro: Write facts another steward can pick up on Monday. Print the intake worksheet and keep it on your device — not on an employer computer.
investigation.worksheetJump: Jump to the printable intake sheet
investigation.tip: Facts first. Name the article, the date, and the remedy before you draft the form.
investigation.leaveOut: Do not write legal conclusions (“this is constructive dismissal”). Keep medical detail out of a grievance file unless the CA and the member require it. Do not promise a win in notes the employer might see.

who.label: Who
who.content: Good notes name roles and shifts: the member (a pseudonym is enough), the supervisor who acted, witnesses who saw it. Leave out character judgments and unrelated complaints about the same people.

what.label: What
what.content: Good notes are observable: what was said, written, or done, in order. Leave out what you think it really means and what should happen next — that belongs in Want.

where.label: Where
where.content: Good notes pin the place: department, room, remote or on site, which campus. Leave out a tour of every other location where similar things always happen.

when.label: When
when.content: Good notes give date and time of the incident and when the member told you. The filing clock usually starts here. Leave out a vague “last week” if you can still pin the day.

why.label: Why
why.content: Good notes cite the CA article, past practice, or statute you believe was broken — quote the clause, do not paraphrase from memory. Leave out a general “this is unfair” with no article.

want.label: Want
want.content: Good notes name a specific remedy: full back pay, the warning pulled from the file, the overtime paid. Leave out “make them sorry” or “we will win at arbitration.”

clocks.title: How to count clocks
clocks.intro: Your CA invents the clocks. Officer Hub tracks them. A missed deadline can kill the file even when the facts are strong.
clocks.warningTitle: Missing a deadline can void the file
clocks.warning: Always confirm exact clocks in your Collective Agreement. Calendar days and working days are not the same. An extension that is not in writing is not an extension.

trigger.label: Find the trigger
trigger.content: Most clocks start when the member knew or ought to have known, or when the employer acted. Write that date on the worksheet the same day you hear the story.

count.label: Calendar vs working days
count.content: Read the article. Some CAs count working days and skip weekends and holidays; others count calendar days. Do not assume “10 days” means two weeks on the wall calendar.

extension.label: Extend in writing
extension.content: If you need more time, get the employer's written agreement before the clock expires. A hallway “sure, take another week” is not a record.

late.label: What a missed deadline does
late.content: Many CAs treat a late filing as abandoned. Flag the risk the same day. Do not wait until after vacation to discover the clock ran out.

steps.title: Your CA names the steps
steps.intro: Informal discussion, a written grievance, and a referral to mediation or arbitration are jobs, not a universal three-step map. Read the article. Copy the names your CA uses onto the file.
steps.example: One Ontario college Support Staff agreement uses four named steps: Step 1, Step 2, Step 3, then Arbitration. Full-time response windows are often 5, 10, and 15 working days; part-time windows are often 7, 14, and 21. Your CA may use different names, different counts, and a different order.

exampleTable.caption: Example employer response windows only — Ontario college Support Staff pattern. Confirm every clock in your Collective Agreement.

informal.title: Informal discussion
informal.body: Many CAs require you and the member to raise the issue with the immediate supervisor first. Log the date, who was in the room, and the answer. If the supervisor refuses or the clock runs, move to the written step your CA names.

written.title: Written grievance
written.body: You file a signed written grievance that states the facts, the article, and the remedy. A meeting follows with the employer representatives your CA names — often HR or a manager above the supervisor.

referral.title: Referral
referral.body: If the employer denies the file, your local executive and servicing representative decide whether to refer it to mediation or binding arbitration. That decision is not automatic. Duty of fair representation governs how you decline.

meeting.title: The grievance meeting
meeting.intro: You are not a silent witness. You are the union in the room.
meeting.warning: Do not let management intimidate the member. When you act as steward, you sit as an equal across the table — not as a guest in their office.

speak.label: Speak for the file
speak.content: Ask what policy or article they rely on. Request specifics. Caucus with the member before anyone signs a statement.

notes.label: Take your own notes
notes.content: Write who said what. Do not rely on the employer's minutes as the only record.

member.label: Protect the member
member.content: Stop a rush to confess. Ask for a break. The goal is an accurate record, not a fast meeting.

workedFile.title: Worked file: one discipline week
workedFile.intro: A member texts Friday night: a written warning landed after a meeting you did not attend. Walk the file in order.

d0.label: Friday night — intake
d0.content: Reply: send the warning and any emails. Do not discuss the file with the supervisor over the weekend. Put the incident date on the worksheet.

d1.label: Monday — 6 W's
d1.content: Interview the member. Cite the discipline article. Name witnesses. Write the remedy: warning removed from the file. Check whether an informal step is still required or already spent.

d3.label: Wednesday — informal or written
d3.content: If the CA still requires an informal raise, do it and log the answer. If the supervisor already issued the warning in writing, file the written grievance on the CA clock.

d7.label: The following week — denial
d7.content: Employer denies. Calendar the next step. Brief the chief steward. If officers later decline to refer, that letter belongs in the DFR playbook — not a hallway no.

workedFile.tip: Copy the spacing: intake the day you hear it, 6 W's before you file, written step on the clock, then a recorded next decision.

failureModes.title: What kills a file
failureModes.intro: Most losses are process, not weak facts. DFR keeps how to decline in writing. This list is how files die before that decision.

missedClock.label: Missed clock
missedClock.content: The article expired while the worksheet sat in a bag. Fix: write the trigger date the same day; put the due date on a calendar the steward on coverage can see.

noArticle.label: No CA article
noArticle.content: The form says “unfair” and names no clause. Fix: quote the article or past practice before you file.

mixedForum.label: Mixed forums
mixedForum.content: A health and safety refusal, a bump, and a discipline grievance in one letter. Fix: pick the forum; file the others on their own clocks.

hallwayPromise.label: Hallway promise
hallwayPromise.content: “We will get this thrown out.” Then the file is denied. Fix: promise process and timelines, not outcomes.

emptyFile.label: Empty file on vacation
emptyFile.content: You leave Friday with notes in your head. Coverage cannot find the clock. Fix: the worksheet and Officer Hub are the shared record.

memberTalk.title: What to tell the member
memberTalk.intro: Good intake conversation prevents hallway promises and DFR complaints later. Plain language, realistic timelines, and a written next step.

promise.label: Do not promise a win
promise.content: Say: “I will investigate, log the facts, and the executive decides whether to file.” Not: “This is a slam dunk” or “They always lose these.”

status.label: Name the next update
status.content: If you promise news by Wednesday, send it — even if the answer is “still waiting on documents.” Silence reads as abandonment.

meeting.label: Prep them for the meeting
meeting.content: Explain who will be in the room, that you may caucus, and that they should not rush to sign employer notes. The goal is an accurate record.

denial.label: If officers later decline to refer
denial.content: Point to the written explanation and the DFR playbook. Do not debate outcomes in a group chat. A hallway no is not a record.

checklist.title: Before you file — quick checklist
checklist.intro: Run this list on paper or in Officer Hub before the written step leaves your hands.

forum.label: Right forum
forum.content: Not a refusal, bump, or joint-table issue dressed up as a grievance.

trigger.label: Trigger date written
trigger.content: Incident date and the date the member told you — same day you hear the story.

article.label: CA article quoted
article.content: Clause number or past-practice reference — not “unfair treatment.”

remedy.label: Remedy named
remedy.content: Specific ask: back pay, warning removed, schedule restored.

worksheet.label: 6 W's complete
worksheet.content: Who, what, where, when, why, want — facts a coverage steward can read cold.

calendar.label: Clock on a calendar
calendar.content: Due date visible to coverage — not only in your head.

coverage.label: Coverage knows
coverage.content: Officer Hub or a shared folder: next step, due date, and your contact.

memberUpdate.label: Member knows the plan
memberUpdate.content: They know the next meeting or update date and what you need from them.

worksheet.title: 6 W's intake sheet (print or export)
worksheet.intro: Use this on your own device during the first interview. Export a blank branded Excel sheet or fill fields in Document Generator before you print.

columns.label: Fields
columns.content: Incident date · CA article · Who · What · Where · When · Why · Want · Witnesses · Clock notes

witness.label: Witnesses and documents
witness.content: List names and what they saw. Attach emails, warnings, or schedules the member can share — not employer systems you cannot access.

footer.label: Footer
footer.content: Steward name, intake date, and Officer Hub case ID once the file is open.

worksheet.exportHint: Opens Document Generator with a blank grievance intake grid ready to export on your device.

tools.title: Printables and next guides
tools.intro: Keep reference material on your device. Confirm clocks in your Collective Agreement — the sources footer lists the finder.

worksheet.label: 6 W's intake sheet
worksheet.content: Blank Excel export for the first interview — same fields as this playbook.

dfr.label: Duty of fair representation
dfr.content: When officers decline to file or refer — written reasons, review paths, and member conversations.

hub.label: Officer Hub grievances
hub.content: Shared clocks and steps once the local uses hosted Hub — not required for the worksheet.

ca.label: Collective Agreement finder
ca.content: Named steps, response windows, and discipline language live in the agreement you actually work under.

diagnostic.label: Complaint vs grievance diagnostic
diagnostic.content: Score five eligibility points, then draft the 6 W's and FAR on your device.

discipline.label: Pre-disciplinary meeting log
discipline.content: Check notice, representation, and disclosure before the interview deepens.

rtw.label: Return-to-work & accommodation
rtw.content: Human-rights primacy, Meiorin test, and functional-limits intake before HR meetings.

hub.title: Hand the file to Officer Hub
hub.body: The worksheet is your on-device record — no login. Officer Hub is the shared clock: steps, due dates, and notes a coverage steward can see. It tracks the CA; it does not invent it.

grievanceGuide.sourcesNote: The Collective Agreement finder, the Colleges Collective Bargaining Act, and the Labour Relations Act show where procedure and the duty live. Duty of fair representation is the other playbook.

workplaceMappingGuide.title: Workplace Mapping & Finding Organic Leaders
workplaceMappingGuide.subtitle: Chart who works where, who listens to whom, and where to spend organizing time
workplaceMappingGuide.intro: Workplace mapping, often called wall charting, is how you understand the real power structure of your workplace. It is not only who works where. It is who listens to whom.

sensitive.title: This is sensitive data
sensitive.body: Because mapping tracks member sentiment, this is sensitive data. Do not store it on employer networks, and do not pin scored names on a public board. Download the template and keep the file on a personal device.

workplaceMappingGuide.downloadHint: Opens in Excel or another spreadsheet app on your own device.

gate.title: When to map, and who holds the file
gate.intro: A map is for organizing density — a membership drive, a contract campaign, or a department that never hears from the union. It is not a substitute for one intake file.

when.label: When to map
when.content: Build it before you ask people to sign or vote. Skip a full map if you only need notes for one member; use Steward 101 instead.

who.label: Who holds it
who.content: Two or three trusted stewards keep the file. Not a group email, not a shared employer drive, and not the local's public cloud account.

never.label: Where it never lives
never.content: Never pin a scored map on a public union board, never store it on employer cloud, and never photograph the wall chart.

gate.warningTitle: A score is not a hit list
gate.warning: Duty of Fair Representation still applies. A 4 gets the same representation as a 1. Mapping tells you where to spend organizing time. It does not decide who you represent.

physical.title: Step 1: The physical map
physical.intro: Start by listing every worker in your unit. Group them by:
physical.diagramLabel: Sample wall chart grouping Student Services, the library, and the front desk across days, nights, and weekends
physical.blindSpot: If you do not know who is in a department, you have found a blind spot in your communication tree.

social.title: Step 2: The social map and organic leaders
social.intro: Management has an official organizational chart. The union needs a social map. You are looking for organic leaders: the people others naturally turn to for advice, gossip, or help.
social.diagramLabel: Social cluster around Priya, an organic leader, with a night-shift blind spot below

items.policy: If a new policy is announced, whose desk does everyone gather around to complain?
items.gifts: Who organizes the retirement gifts or birthday cards?
items.newHires: Who do the new hires go to when they do not understand how to do their job?

social.goal: Your goal is to recruit these organic leaders. If you win over one organic leader, you win over the five to ten people who listen to them.

scale.title: Step 3: The 1-to-5 assessment scale
scale.intro: Once you have your map, honestly assess where every worker stands. Use this standard organizing scale:
scale.diagramLabel: Union support scale from 1 organizer through 5 unknown

one.label: 1: The organizer.
one.content: Actively volunteers, comes to meetings, and brings others along.

two.label: 2: The supporter.
two.content: Votes yes, wears the button, and supports the union, but will not actively lead or organize.

three.label: 3: Undecided or neutral.
three.content: Does not know much about the union, is scared of management, or does not care. This is where you spend most of your organizing time.

four.label: 4: Anti-union.
four.content: Vocally opposes the union and defends management. Do not waste time arguing with 4s.

five.label: 5: Unknown.
five.content: You do not know where they stand. Your immediate goal is a 1-on-1 conversation to turn this 5 into a 1, 2, 3, or 4.

scale.spend: Spend organizing time on 3s and on 5s you have not met. Recruit 1s and 2s who are already organic leaders. Do not argue with 4s.

conversations.title: 1-on-1 conversations
conversations.intro: A 5 stays a 5 until someone talks with them. Keep the conversation short, listen first, and update the map the same day.

listen.label: Listen
listen.content: Ask what is going on in their area. Do not pitch the union before you have heard the issue they already care about.

connect.label: Connect
connect.content: Name that issue, then how the union already acts on it — a clause, a grievance, or a meeting they can join.

ask.label: Ask
ask.content: If they are ready, ask them to join or to bring one coworker to the next conversation. One ask, then stop.

log.label: Log it
log.content: Update the score the same day. A 5 you talked to is no longer a 5.

conversations.tip: Take a 1 or a 2 with you when you talk to a 3. Organic leaders open doors that a steward badge does not.

worked.title: Worked example: Student Services days
worked.intro: Fictional Student Services day shift. Names and scores are teaching only — not a real workplace.

list.label: Week 0, list everyone
list.content: Write every name on days and nights. You already know the day-shift cluster; nights are still blank.

leader.label: Find the organic leader
leader.content: Coworkers gather at Priya's desk after policy emails. Mark her as an organic leader and a 2.

ones.label: Run the 1-on-1s
ones.content: Listen to Sam about dues. Ask Alex, who has never been asked. Do not debate Riley in the lunchroom.

nights.label: Name the blind spot
nights.content: Nights still have no assigned steward. Quinn is the night-shift organic leader; Morgan is still a 5.

table.caption: Teaching example — fictional names, not a real workplace. Download the same rows as a spreadsheet in the files section.

priya.name: Priya N.
priya.notes: Coworkers gather at her desk after policy emails

casey.name: Casey L.
casey.notes: New hire; asked Priya how to do the job

morgan.name: Morgan D.
morgan.notes: Blind spot — no steward on nights

worked.tip: Jordan (a 1) should take the next 1-on-1 with Sam. Priya (a 2) is the person Casey already trusts.

keep.title: Keep the map alive — and private
keep.intro: A map that is six months old is a rumour. Update it after 1-on-1s, and keep paper and files where members and managers cannot browse them.

update.label: Update the same day
update.content: After every 1-on-1, change the score that day. Stale maps lie.

paper.label: Paper stays locked
paper.content: A paper wall chart belongs in a locked private room, not on the cork members walk past.

photo.label: Never photograph it
photo.content: A phone photo is a leak waiting to be forwarded. Copy names by hand if you must move the chart.

review.label: Revisit before a drive
review.content: Look again before a membership drive or a vote. Blind spots — nights, weekends, satellite sites — are the next organizing work.

reference.title: Files and related tools
reference.intro: Use the blank sheet for your workplace. Use the sample sheet to see a filled row. Org Chart prints who to contact; it is not a place for scores.

blank.title: Blank workplace map
blank.body: Empty spreadsheet with the eight columns. Fill it on a personal device, never on employer cloud.

example.title: Sample Student Services chart
example.body: The fictional rows from the table above, with the same column headers as the blank file. Rewrite every name for your own workplace.

orgChart.title: Org Chart is not this map
orgChart.body: Org Chart prints officers and stewards for a public board. Mapping scores stay off that cork. Use Org Chart for names and roles; keep this spreadsheet on a personal device.

membership.title: When a 5 becomes a 2
membership.body: Walk the membership signup playbook — card, witness, and steward follow-up. Do not store signed cards in the same file as scores.

privacy.title: Privacy warning
privacy.body: Never build your map on a work computer, employer-provided Office 365, or an employer Google Drive account. Keep mapping files on your local, personal device to protect your members.

seniorityGuide.title: Seniority & bumping playbook
seniorityGuide.subtitle: Seniority worksheets for bumping files. Aid only.
seniorityGuide.intro: Bumping files turn on seniority dates, classification boundaries, and posting rules — not debate energy. This playbook walks stewards through comparing two members, mapping one- and two-step cascades, and running a committee meeting with the worksheet. Verify every rule against your CA.

disclaimer.title: Not legal advice. Aid only.
disclaimer.body: Not a calculator and not legal advice. Confirm dates and rights against the CA and local practice.

gate.title: Before you open a bumping file
gate.intro: Posting disputes, layoff bumps, and classification grievances share vocabulary but not the same procedure. Run this gate so the committee does not debate the wrong problem.

bumping.label: Is this a layoff or displacement bump?
bumping.content: A bumping file applies when the CA lets a displaced member claim a lower or lateral role by seniority during a layoff or restructuring. You need a vacancy chain, not just “I wanted that posting.”

posting.label: Is this only a posting complaint?
posting.content: If the issue is whether a vacancy was posted correctly or qualifications were applied fairly, start with posting articles and may be a grievance — not a seniority committee ranking session.

grievance.label: Already filed as a grievance?
grievance.content: If a formal grievance is live on the same facts, coordinate with the steward handling it. Do not let the committee pre-judge an outcome the grievance path owns.

committee.label: Does the CA require a committee?
committee.content: Some collections require a seniority committee vote; others are steward-led with employer notice. Confirm who chairs, who records, and what happens if the committee cannot agree.

gate.warning: Pause the meeting. Read the layoff, posting, and seniority articles together. A posting grievance dressed as a bump wastes everyone's seniority dates.

compare.title: Worked example: two members, one target role
compare.intro: Role “Facilities Coordinator” is eliminated. Member A and Member B both claim bump into posted “Maintenance Clerk.” Write dates before anyone argues qualifications.

setup.label: Set up the sheet
setup.content: Two rows only: Member A and Member B. Columns for seniority date, classification, current role, and target role. No names from other campuses yet.

dates.label: Enter sample dates
dates.content: Member A — seniority 2014-03-12, Maintenance Lead. Member B — seniority 2016-09-01, Facilities Coordinator (eliminated). Target: Maintenance Clerk (posted 2026-02-01).

clock.label: Confirm which clock the CA uses
clock.content: Open the CA: is this continuous service, classification seniority, or another date? If B's elimination triggers bumping rights, note the article before comparing.

tie.label: Break ties on paper
tie.content: If dates tie, write the CA tie-break (hire number, draw, hours in classification). Do not assume “longer in the building” wins without the article.

qualify.label: Then check qualifications
qualify.content: Only after seniority order is drafted, mark Yes, No, or Unknown on ability, licensing, and posting eligibility. A more senior member who fails ability may not hold the bump.

compare.tip: If you cannot write both seniority dates and the target role on one row each, you are not ready to vote.

cascade1.title: Worked example: two-person chain
cascade1.intro: One vacancy, one bumper, one displaced incumbent. Map this before calling a three-deep scenario.

vacancy.label: Start with the vacancy
vacancy.content: Maintenance Clerk posted and filled — then the layoff removes Facilities Coordinator (Member B). The bump target is the clerk role Member B wants.

bumper.label: Name the bumper
bumper.content: Member B (2016-09-01) claims bump into Maintenance Clerk. Confirm B is in the right classification and meets ability language.

displaced.label: Name who gets displaced
displaced.content: Member C (2019-11-15) currently holds Maintenance Clerk — the incumbent B would displace. C may have their own bump rights into another posted role.

floor.label: Mark the floor
floor.content: If C cannot bump further — probation, temporary status, or CA floor — write “chain ends at C” on the worksheet. Stop inventing extra steps.

log.label: Log the step
log.content: Committee log line: “B bumps to Clerk, displacing C — articles cited, next meeting date if C claims further bump.”

cascade2.title: Worked example: Members A, B, and C
cascade2.intro: Role X vacant, Role Y posted. A three-deep chain displaces two incumbents. Map every hop before anyone signs.

roleX.label: Vacancy at Role X
roleX.content: Lab Technician II (Role X) is eliminated in a layoff. The posted replacement path runs through Role Y (Lab Technician I).

memberA.label: Member A — first bumper
memberA.content: Member A (2013-06-01, Lab Tech I) is most senior eligible and claims bump into Role X. A meets classification and ability for X.

memberB.label: Member B — displaced incumbent
memberB.content: Member B (2015-02-14) held Role X and bumps into posted Role Y (Lab Tech I) if seniority and classification allow.

memberC.label: Member C — last link
memberC.content: Member C (2018-10-30) holds Role Y. Confirm whether C can bump into a posted Role Z or hits a CA floor (probation, temp, or classification boundary).

worksheet.label: Worksheet one row per hop
worksheet.content: Rows: A → X, B → Y, C → ? Mark “chain ends here” beside C if no further bump. Alternate candidates get a blank row — not a side debate.

cascade2.tip: If you cannot name A, B, and C with dates on the worksheet, postpone the vote.

meeting.title: How to run the seniority committee
meeting.intro: A disciplined meeting beats a long argument. Use the worksheet as the agenda — not as decoration.

open.label: Open with the CA articles
open.content: Chair reads the layoff, bumping, and committee articles aloud. Note which collection (FT/PT/support) applies before any names.

worksheet.label: Project or pass the worksheet
worksheet.content: Every person in the chain gets a row. Stewards fill dates; members confirm or challenge with documents — not memory.

oneChain.label: Resolve one chain at a time
oneChain.content: Finish Role X → Y → Z before opening a second vacancy. Mixing chains on one sheet causes transposed dates.

vote.label: Vote on facts, then outcome
vote.content: First agree seniority order and eligibility flags. Then vote the bump outcome. Dissents go in the log with the member's name and reason.

minutes.label: Minutes = worksheet + decision
minutes.content: Attach the completed worksheet (or Hub export) to minutes: date, chair, attendees, articles cited, and “chain ends at Member C.”

file.label: File one copy in the case
file.content: Steward keeps the signed worksheet in the bumping file and links the Officer Hub case ID if your local uses College Bumping.

meeting.tip: If the room argues qualifications before dates are on the sheet, call a five-minute break and reset.

pitfalls.title: Common pitfalls
pitfalls.intro: Most committee errors come from mixing clocks or ignoring boundaries the CA already defines.

postingDate.label: Posting date vs. seniority date
postingDate.content: A vacancy posted 2026-02-01 is not someone's seniority. Do not rank members by posting date.

classification.label: Classification boundaries
classification.content: FT/PT or support-staff collections may not bump across freely. Confirm the collection before ranking.

probation.label: Probationary or temporary status
probation.content: Confirm bumping rights before ranking someone. Probation and temp status often block bumps entirely.

earlierWins.label: “Earlier date always wins”
earlierWins.content: Read tie-break and ability language. Seniority order is necessary — not always sufficient.

worksheet.title: Paper worksheet (print or export)
worksheet.intro: Use this column layout on a blank page, spreadsheet, or branded export during the meeting. Keep one signed copy in the case file.

columns.label: Columns
columns.content: Member ref · Seniority date · Classification · Current position · Target / bump claim · Eligible? (Y/N/?) · Notes / CA article

rows.label: Rows
rows.content: One per person in the chain, plus a blank row for alternate candidates. Mark “chain ends here” when the CA blocks another bump.

footer.label: Footer
footer.content: Session date, chair, decision summary, and Officer Hub bumping case ID if your local uses one.

worksheet.exportHint: Opens Document Generator with a blank branded seniority grid ready to export.

hub.title: Officer Hub bumping module
hub.body: In the Officer Hub, College Bumping keeps your notes, PDF comparisons, and sessions in one place. Treat any ranking aid as a double-check, and re-run the paper worksheet if a result surprises you.

jointCommitteeGuide.title: Joint committee playbook
jointCommitteeGuide.subtitle: From a campus issue to a provincial table recommendation — and a member note members can actually use
jointCommitteeGuide.intro: Joint labour-management committees recommend; they do not bargain and they do not hear live grievances. This playbook is for union-side volunteers who need to move a system-wide issue from campus to a provincial table, keep caucus strategy private, and explain signed minutes to members without re-hosting the official record.

disclaimer.title: Not the official record. Not legal advice.
disclaimer.body: Management usually records joint minutes. Both parties post the signed copy. UnionOps helps with union caucus prep and member explainers — not minute-taking, not employer login, and not a substitute for your servicing rep.

gate.title: Before you book a joint meeting
gate.intro: Wrong forum wastes months. Run this gate on every new item before you put it on a joint agenda.

grievance.label: Already a formal grievance?
grievance.content: Stop. Joint committees must refuse items that are in the grievance procedure. Route through stewards and the grievance path instead — see the DFR guide for intake discipline.

local.label: Has campus already tried?
local.content: Provincial tables expect a local union-college or labour-management committee to have met first. You need dates, attendees, and what the employer said before you refer up.

system.label: Is it system-wide?
system.content: Joint committees handle problems that cross campuses or need a provincial recommendation to bargaining — not one manager’s scheduling habit on a single floor.

hs.label: Is this really health and safety?
hs.content: JHSC and a joint EERC-style table are different bodies. Hazards and refusals go through OHSA and your JHSC; policy and workload patterns may fit a joint committee after local attempts.

gate.warning: Do not put the item on a provincial joint agenda to “see what happens.” Fix the path first — local committee, grievance, or JHSC — or you risk burning trust on both sides of the table.

localFirst.title: Step 1 — local union-college committee
localFirst.intro: Document the campus attempt before you ask for provincial time. Principals and co-chairs will ask what already happened locally.

schedule.label: Schedule the local meeting
schedule.content: Book the campus union-college or labour-management committee. Bring the member’s facts in writing — dates, emails, CA articles, and the ask.

record.label: Record what was said
record.content: Note who attended, what the employer answered, and whether they agreed to fix, study, or refuse. Neutral notes only — not your provincial strategy.

deadline.label: Set a follow-up date
deadline.content: If the employer asks for time, put a return date in writing. Silence is not a solution you can refer upward.

refer.label: Package the referral
refer.content: If local fails or stalls, draft a one-page referral: issue, local dates, employer response, and why it needs a provincial look. Your co-chair sends it through union channels.

localFirst.tip: If you cannot name a local meeting date and outcome, you are not ready for a provincial slot.

referUp.title: Step 2 — provincial referral package
referUp.intro: Provincial joint tables are scarce meeting time. Send a tight package so union co-chairs can place the item without re-interviewing the member.

facts.label: One-page fact summary
facts.content: What happened, how many campuses are affected, which CA articles apply, and what you want the committee to recommend.

localLog.label: Local attempt log
localLog.content: Dates of campus meetings, employer attendees, and responses. Attach redacted emails if you have them.

ask.label: Clear union ask
ask.content: Recommend to bargaining? Request a joint letter? Ask the employer council to study? Name the outcome — not “raise awareness.”

notify.label: Tell the other party
notify.content: The CA expects notice before you refer. Do not surprise management at the provincial table.

caucus.title: Step 3 — union caucus before the joint table
caucus.intro: Meet your side alone. Caucus notes are strategy — never joint minutes, never employer-visible.

ask.label: Agree the ask and red lines
ask.content: What you want, what you can trade, and what is non-negotiable. If you cannot state the ask in one sentence, postpone the joint meeting.

roles.label: Assign roles
roles.content: Speaker, note-taker, timekeeper, and who follows up with locals after. One voice in the room beats five partial stories.

brief.label: Draft the union brief
brief.content: Use Document Generator letterhead for the union-side speaking notes. Do not paste caucus notes into the joint record.

private.label: Keep caucus private
private.content: Use a Local Portal Circle or an in-person huddle — invite union side only. Never invite the employer into caucus space.

caucus.tip: If caucus notes could be mistaken for official minutes, rewrite them. Strategy leaks destroy the next meeting.

jointTable.title: Step 4 — at the joint table
jointTable.intro: The committee recommends to bargaining or another named body. Management records the major subjects; co-chairs sign. Drafts stay inside the committee until both sides agree.

refuse.label: Refuse grievances
refuse.content: If the item slipped through as a live grievance, stop and re-route. The table is not a grievance hearing.

speak.label: Stick to the agreed ask
speak.content: Speaker delivers the union brief. Others add facts only when asked. Debate management spin in caucus, not across the table.

minutes.label: Correct draft minutes
minutes.content: Management drafts. Send corrections through your co-chair in writing — factual fixes only, not argument.

consensus.label: Consensus or separate briefs
consensus.content: If you agree, the recommendation goes to the body named in your CA. If not, each side may send its own brief through its co-chair.

noBargain.label: Do not bargain here
noBargain.content: Workload caps, wages, and language changes belong at bargaining unless the CA explicitly routes them through this committee.

jointTable.warning: Do not post draft minutes to locals, boards, or social. Members wait for the signed copy on the official union and employer-council sites.

afterMinutes.title: Step 5 — after minutes are signed
afterMinutes.intro: Point members at the official posting, then explain in plain language what changed and what they should do next.

link.label: Link the official minutes
link.content: Use the union-side and employer-council URLs from the sources block. Do not re-host the PDF on a local site as if UnionOps were the publisher.

note.label: Write the member note
note.content: Three parts: what was asked, what the committee decided, what happens next. One contact for follow-up — not a comment-thread debate.

locals.label: Brief affected locals
locals.content: Letterhead to presidents or stewards on campuses that raised the issue. Include the same link and ask.

comms.label: Comms only after approval
comms.content: Flyer or board notice after minutes are signed — never from a draft. See the email outreach guide for copy-only sends without marketing lists.

afterMinutes.tip: Subject line example: “Provincial committee update — workload review referred to bargaining.” Body: three sentences and one official link.

fullScenario.title: Worked walk-through: overtime emails to a member note
fullScenario.intro: Members at three campuses report mandatory overtime scheduling by email outside CA posting rules. No grievance is filed yet — this is a system-wide pattern.

w1.label: Week 1 — campus committees
w1.content: Each local UCC meets. Stewards bring redacted emails and CA posting articles. Employer asks for two weeks to “review centrally.” Locals log dates and attendees.

w3.label: Week 3 — referral fails locally
w3.content: Two campuses get no follow-up; one gets a vague reply. Union co-chairs package a provincial referral: fact summary, local log, union ask for a joint recommendation to bargaining.

w5.label: Week 5 — caucus and joint table
w5.content: Union caucus agrees ask: recommend standardized posting windows. Speaker uses letterhead brief. Joint table records consensus to refer to bargaining teams; management drafts minutes.

w7.label: Week 7 — signed minutes and member note
w7.content: Co-chairs sign. Union and employer council post PDFs. Union comms sends a three-sentence note with both links and steward contact — no draft language, no negotiation details.

fullScenario.tip: If your timeline skips campus attempts, expect the provincial co-chair to send it back.

caArticles.title: Where to look in the CA (Ontario college example)
caArticles.intro: Article numbers differ by collection. Open your CA from the sources below — do not rely on memory.

pt.label: Part-time Support Staff
pt.content: Article 5.4 and Appendix 4 — Employee/Employer Relations Committee. Local issues after UCC; management records minutes; both parties post signed copies.

ft.label: Full-time Support Staff
ft.content: Article 4.7 and Appendix J — same committee shape for the FT collection. Meeting frequency and travel rules differ — read the appendix.

other.label: Other unions
other.content: Find your joint-committee article and appendix the same way. The campus → caucus → table → signed minutes path still applies.

notThis.title: What joint committees are not
notThis.intro: Volunteers often sit on more than one committee. Keep the roles separate.

grievance.label: Not a grievance forum
grievance.content: Live grievances stay in the grievance procedure. Officer Hub grievance tools track those files — not joint committee dockets.

jhsc.label: Not the JHSC
jhsc.content: Workplace hazards and OHSA refusals go through health-and-safety representation and the right-to-refuse guide.

lec.label: Not the LEC
lec.content: Local executive runs the local — elections, finances, and steward coordination. Joint tables are provincial or divisional recommenders.

bargain.label: Not the bargaining table
bargain.content: Committees recommend to bargaining teams; they do not settle wage or language packages.

tools.title: Tools for union-side work
tools.intro: Use Comms tools after signed minutes or for union-only drafts. Hub snippets and grievances stay separate from joint table items.

letterhead.label: Letterhead and briefs
letterhead.content: Document Generator letterhead for union caucus briefs and local referral packages.

explainer.label: Member explainer
explainer.content: Flyer Maker or Graphic Maker after minutes are public — one ask, one official link.

email.label: Email to locals
email.content: Email outreach guide for copy-only sends — no marketing lists.

portal.label: Multi-local caucus
portal.content: Local Portal Circle with members from more than one local — union invitees only.

example.title: One Ontario example
example.body: College support staff at OPSEU / SEFPO have provincial Employee/Employer Relations Committees (PT and FT collections). The CA says management records minutes and both parties post the signed copy. Use the sources below — the same playbook fits other joint committees in other unions.

portal.title: Local Portal for a caucus from more than one local
portal.body: If your union uses Local Portal, create a Circle and tick members from more than one local. Invite the union side only. Hall still belongs to one local. Public Comms tools stay free on your device either way.

rightToRefuseGuide.title: Right to refuse unsafe work
rightToRefuseGuide.subtitle: OHSA s.43 refusal steps for stewards and JHSC members. Not legal advice.
rightToRefuseGuide.intro: Ontario OHSA s.43 gives workers a structured refusal path — report, employer investigation, then ministry inspector if the danger persists. This playbook is for stewards and JHSC worker members who need to support a member without mixing up grievance, JHSC hazard work, and the live refusal procedure. Confirm against current legislation and the ministry Part V guide in the sources below.

disclaimer.title: Not legal advice
disclaimer.body: Procedure overview only. Confirm with JHSC practice, local officers, and current OHSA text.

gate.title: Before you advise — pick the right path
gate.intro: A hazard report, a live refusal, and a scheduling grievance need different forums. Run this gate before you tell a member what to do next.

ohsa.label: Is someone refusing work right now?
ohsa.content: OHSA s.43 applies when a worker believes work is likely to endanger them or another person. Follow the refusal stages in this guide — report, stay available, stage 1 investigation, then stage 2 inspector if needed.

jhsc.label: Is this a hazard to fix, not a live refusal?
jhsc.content: JHSC inspects, recommends, and tracks hazards under the internal responsibility system. A member can report through JHSC without refusing work — but once they refuse, the s.43 clock runs separately from committee meetings.

grievance.label: Is this really a CA or discipline issue?
grievance.content: Forced overtime, bullying, or contract violations may be grievances — not refusals. Do not tell a member to “refuse” as a shortcut around the grievance procedure unless a genuine safety danger exists.

both.label: Can both paths run?
both.content: Yes — a live refusal can overlap with a JHSC recommendation or a grievance about reprisal. Keep files separate: OHSA notes with times and witnesses; grievance facts with CA articles.

gate.warning: Routing a contract dispute through a refusal, or treating a live refusal as “just a JHSC item,” burns trust and can leave the member without pay or protection. Fix the path first.

ontarioScope.title: Ontario scope (read this first)
ontarioScope.intro: OHSA s.43 covers most provincially regulated Ontario workplaces, with exceptions. Verify coverage for your workplace type before advising.

coverage.label: Label training materials
coverage.content: Mark this guide Ontario-only in any local training handout you reprint. Other provinces and federal workplaces use different refusal frameworks.

federal.label: Federal and other provinces
federal.content: Federal workplaces and other provinces follow different refusal frameworks. Do not assume Ontario steps apply on another jurisdiction's shop floor.

modified.label: Modified rights
modified.content: Some worker categories have modified rights under the Act. Check current OHSA text and ministry materials before advising police, firefighters, or other listed groups.

unionRole.label: Union role
unionRole.content: Union representation supports the member at investigation steps where the Act allows. It does not replace the JHSC worker member or the ministry inspector's role.

stageOne.title: Stage 1 — report and employer investigation
stageOne.intro: A worker who believes work is likely to endanger them (or another) may refuse. Report promptly. Do not walk out in silence.

report.label: Report to supervisor / employer
report.content: The worker promptly reports the circumstances — what task, what hazard, who else is affected. Stewards help the member state facts, not slogans.

safePlace.label: Stay in a safe place nearby
safePlace.content: The worker remains available for investigation steps. Leaving campus without notice can be treated as abandonment — confirm local practice with your president.

accompany.label: Accompany where the Act allows
accompany.content: The worker may be accompanied by a JHSC worker member or union health-and-safety rep during the employer investigation. Stewards: confirm your right to be present before the meeting starts.

investigate.label: Employer investigates in presence of worker
investigate.content: The employer investigates with the worker and worker representative present. Take notes: start time, attendees, hazard described, interim controls offered.

stewardNotes.label: Steward notes for the local file
stewardNotes.content: Record the member's exact words on the hazard, photos if safe, SDS sheets for chemicals, and whether the employer stopped work or offered alternate tasks.

resolve.label: If resolved, document
resolve.content: If the danger is fixed or the worker agrees it is resolved, work may resume — but write the outcome: who said what, what changed, date and time. Do not rely on verbal “it's fine now.”

stageOne.tip: If the member has not reported to a supervisor yet, your first job is getting the report on the record — not debating whether the hazard is real.

stageTwo.title: Stage 2 — ministry inspector
stageTwo.intro: When the worker still believes the danger exists after stage 1, the matter escalates to a Ministry of Labour, Immigration, Training and Skills Development inspector.

trigger.label: When stage 2 opens
trigger.content: Stage 2 starts when the worker continues to believe the danger exists after the employer's stage 1 investigation. The member does not need to accept “we disagree.”

whoCalls.label: Who can notify the inspector
whoCalls.content: The employer, the worker, or a JHSC member can notify the ministry. Stewards: know the ministry contact path before the shift — do not waste hours searching mid-refusal.

inspector.label: Inspector investigates
inspector.content: The inspector investigates and decides whether the refusal is likely to endanger. Stay factual. Provide times, witnesses, and documents — not advocacy speeches.

stewardRecords.label: What stewards record
stewardRecords.content: Inspector name/badge if shown, arrival time, who was interviewed, orders or directions given, and whether work resumed. Photo the posted order if one is issued.

factsOnly.label: Facts only — no invented hazards
factsOnly.content: Do not coach members to invent hazards. Misrepresentation hurts the member and the local. If the hazard is weak, say so in caucus — do not fabricate.

stageTwo.warning: If stage 1 ended with “just do the task” and the member still believes they are in danger, stage 2 is not optional politeness — it is the statutory escalation path.

reassignment.title: Work reassignment and pay while the refusal is live
reassignment.intro: While a refusal is active, reassignment and pay rules protect both the refusing worker and anyone else asked to do the work. Verify current Act language before advising.

inform.label: Inform the next worker
inform.content: Other workers assigned the same task must be told a refusal is in progress and why. No silent reassignment — the next person inherits the same hazard without knowing.

pay.label: Pay status of refusing worker
pay.content: The refusing worker is typically paid pending the investigation outcome, subject to current OHSA rules. Track pay on the first shift — do not discover a docked cheque weeks later.

noSilent.label: No pressure to “just do it”
noSilent.content: Supervisors cannot use reassignment to bypass the refusal. If someone else is sent in without being informed, document it for the inspector and the local file.

board.label: Post contacts on the board
board.content: Keep current JHSC contacts, steward numbers, and hazard-reporting steps on the union board — link to live e-Laws, not a faded 2019 photocopy.

reprisal.title: Reprisal and urgent escalation
reprisal.intro: OHSA prohibits reprisals for exercising refusal rights. Treat suspected reprisal as urgent — not a routine grievance delay.

document.label: Document everything tied to the refusal date
document.content: Discipline, schedule changes, harassment, exclusion from shifts, or “performance” meetings within days of the refusal — write dates, names, and exact words.

sameDay.label: Same-day escalation
sameDay.content: Alleged reprisal goes to the local president and union health-and-safety rep the same day. Do not wait for the next stewards' meeting.

sources.label: Pair with official sources
sources.content: Use the ministry Part V walkthrough and live e-Laws s.43 text alongside this guide. Stewards cite procedure; lawyers cite orders.

notRoutine.label: Not a routine grievance timeline
notRoutine.content: Reprisal can overlap grievance and OHSA complaint paths. Parallel tracks are normal — “we filed a grievance” is not an excuse to delay a reprisal response.

reprisal.warning: A member who refused and then gets disciplined needs the same urgency as the original hazard. Document today; escalate today.

fullScenario.title: Worked walk-through: chemical exposure refusal
fullScenario.intro: A custodian is told to mix two cleaning products in a poorly ventilated storage room. They smell strong fumes, feel light-headed, and refuse to continue. No grievance is filed — this is a live OHSA refusal.

t0.label: Shift start — hazard appears
t0.content: Member reports dizziness and fumes to the supervisor at 09:15. Steward arrives by 09:30. Member stays in the hallway — available, not on task.

t1.label: Stage 1 — employer investigation (same day)
t1.content: Supervisor, JHSC worker member, and steward meet at 10:00. Employer offers a different rag and open door — member says danger persists without ventilation and compatible SDS review. Notes taken; SDS photographed.

t2.label: Stage 2 — inspector called (same day)
t2.content: Member still refuses at 11:00. JHSC worker member notifies the ministry. Inspector arrives afternoon; interviews member and supervisor; orders ventilation check before work resumes.

t3.label: Reassignment — another worker not informed
t3.content: At 14:00 a temp is sent to finish the room without being told of the refusal. Steward documents; informs the temp; adds note to inspector file.

t4.label: Follow-up — pay and board
t4.content: Member paid for the shift. Local posts pocket-card QR with s.43 steps and JHSC contacts. Reprisal watch for 30 days — no discipline entries tied to the refusal date.

fullScenario.tip: If your timeline skips the written report or stage 1 attendance list, rebuild it before the inspector interview.

stewardChecklist.title: Before, during, and after a refusal
stewardChecklist.intro: Use this checklist on paper or in the local file. One refusal handled cleanly prevents three bad precedents.

beforeKnow.label: Before — know the path
beforeKnow.content: Read s.43 summary, JHSC contacts, and ministry notification route before your next shift — not after the member calls.

beforeContacts.label: Before — pocket card on the board
beforeContacts.content: QR pocket card preset posted with stage 1 and 2 steps. Link to live e-Laws OHSA text.

duringPresent.label: During — be present at stage 1
duringPresent.content: Attend the employer investigation when the Act allows. Take neutral notes: times, names, hazard as member described it.

duringNotes.label: During — separate OHSA and grievance notes
duringNotes.content: If a grievance may follow, start a separate file. Do not mix “the supervisor is always like this” into the inspector timeline.

afterFile.label: After — close the file
afterFile.content: Write outcome: resumed work, alternate task, inspector order, or ongoing stage 2. Attach pay confirmation and any ministry documentation.

afterBoard.label: After — debrief without names
afterBoard.content: Stewards' council debrief on lessons — ventilation, SDS, reassignment — without identifying the member on a public board.

boards.title: Union boards and pocket cards
boards.body: Keep JHSC contacts and a short hazard / refusal strip on the board. Link QR posters to official e-Laws OHSA text, not outdated photocopies.
boards.exportHint: Opens QR Link Cards with the Ontario right-to-refuse procedure preset — print PNG/PDF for wallets or boards.
