bylaw-builder-committee.body: Draft bylaws article by article with committee notes, paste current text for a redline summary, and load OPSEU / SEFPO college defaults from the Local Bylaws guide.

brand-preset-audit.title: Brand Kit — union preset colours and slogans
brand-preset-audit.body: Union presets now use verified starter colours (CUPE pink from national site assets, PSAC Pantone 1805 red, USW PMS 122U gold, Unifor red and blue), tap-to-apply slogan suggestions in English and French, and closer canvas typefaces when you pick a preset.

running-meetings-guide.title: Running meetings — full guide + cheat sheet
running-meetings-guide.body: The Running a Meeting guide now covers quorum, motion precedence, debate, voting, and a worked GMM example. The Rules of Order cheat sheet adds fourteen actions with chair notes and a copy button for the floor.

land-acknowledgement-guide.title: Land Acknowledgement Guide
land-acknowledgement-guide.body: Learn why acknowledgements matter, research whose traditional territory you are on, and pair words with action — with links to Native-Land.ca, Whose Land, NCTR, and Crown–Indigenous Relations. No script generator.

guide-tool-aside.title: Guides — tool shortcuts on desktop
guide-tool-aside.body: Playbook guides now show Open a tool in the sidebar on wider screens — jump straight to worksheets, QR cards, and flyers without scrolling to the bottom.

guide-playbook-layout.title: Steward playbooks — easier to read on desktop
guide-playbook-layout.body: Labour playbooks now use a sidebar table of contents on wider screens so you can jump sections without losing your place. Phone layout stays the same.

workplace-mapping-guide.title: Workplace mapping and organic leaders
workplace-mapping-guide.body: Chart every coworker by department and shift, find organic leaders, and score support from 1 to 5. Use the sample wall chart, 1-on-1s, and a spreadsheet on a personal device.

board-notice-layouts.title: Board Notice Maker — logo and layouts
board-notice-layouts.body: Pick stack, band, or split layouts, choose none/lockup/mark logo, and export workplace notices that match your Brand Kit.

canvas-logo-mode.title: Logo control on canvas tools
canvas-logo-mode.body: Every canvas tool now shares none/lockup/mark logo plus a Show local number toggle — turn the label off for mark-only visuals.

officer-learning-center.title: Officer Learning — definitive floor path
officer-learning-center.body: Six bilingual modules with a live learning path, teaching diagrams, tickable floor checklists, printable FAR sheets, and links into steward tools and peer guides.

steward-playbooks-hub.title: Steward playbooks hub
steward-playbooks-hub.body: One front door for Steward 101, Officer Learning self-tests, and every floor playbook — with a linked training path diagram.

officer-learning-pocket-pdfs.title: Officer Learning — scenarios, timelines, and pocket sheets
officer-learning-pocket-pdfs.body: Each module now has six quiz questions, a D0–D7 worked-file timeline, Apply/Don't apply scenario frames, printable take-to-meeting sheets, and links from matching floor playbooks.

steward-101-modules.title: Steward 101 — modules, toolkit, and Brand Kit exports
steward-101-modules.body: Four time-boxed modules, a floor toolkit with pocket-card and intake exports, and a Brand Kit nudge so printables show your local number.

steward-101-guide.title: Steward 101: Your Role and Rights
steward-101-guide.body: A foundational floor guide to the three hats, representation rights in discipline meetings, and the duty of fair representation.

grievance-process-guide.title: The Steward's Guide to Grievances
grievance-process-guide.body: A floor playbook with a forum picker, 6 W's intake sheet, example step table, open-file checklist, and member-talk tips. Confirm clocks in your Collective Agreement.

assets-pwa-download.title: Brand Assets stay in the installed app
assets-pwa-download.body: Downloading a logo from Brand Assets no longer opens a new tab that kicks you out of the home-screen shortcut. On the phone you get the share sheet; on desktop the file still saves as before.

labour-guides-rewrite.title: Steward and comms playbooks rewritten
labour-guides-rewrite.body: The Blueprint, labour guides, Strike, and Photo Consent now walk real scenarios — four channels, a sample comms week, decision gates, and tool links you can use on the floor.

graphic-gradient-ink.title: Cleaner graphic backgrounds
graphic-gradient-ink.body: Picket, thanks, spotlight, and results graphics use a solid brand colour with light depth — not multi-colour washes that muddy the plate. Type stays light over a short bottom lift.

federation-sources.title: OFL, NUPGE, and CLC in Sources
federation-sources.body: Comms Resources now points to the Ontario Federation of Labour, NUPGE, and the Canadian Labour Congress for movement education. The same links appear on membership, boards, Blueprint, and crisis guides — and in the website ZIP footer.

joint-committee-guide.title: Joint committee playbook
joint-committee-guide.body: Walk a campus issue to the provincial table, keep union caucus notes private, then explain signed minutes to members with letterhead, flyers, and email.

portal-union-circles.title: Circles for more than one local
portal-union-circles.body: In Local Portal, tick members from more than one local when you create a committee Circle. Invite the union side from other locals. Hall still belongs to one local.

caat-s-gold-plate.title: Coral or gold for College Support
caat-s-gold-plate.body: In Brand Kit, College Support coral and gold appear as separate Look cards. Pick gold for the gold campaign field and white-and-coral lockup, or coral for the coral field.

caat-s-look.title: College Support Look in Brand Kit
caat-s-look.body: College Support locals can pick the CAAT-S coral Look in Brand Kit, or keep national OPSEU / SEFPO blue. Brand Assets now ships every colour and plate variant for download — ready for boards, social, and campaigns.

org-chart.title: Org Chart for the union board
org-chart.body: Print a who-to-contact poster, save officers and stewards as JSON or CSV after elections, and reuse those names on Website Template.

caat-support-collection.title: College Support is one collection
caat-support-collection.body: College Support locals now start with one collection in Brand Kit. Full-time and part-time members share the same local. Membership still has Full-Time and Part-Time join links.

website-config-roundtrip.title: Reopen a downloaded local site
website-config-roundtrip.body: Website Template can import the site file from a ZIP you already downloaded, so you can update officers or copy and download a fresh ZIP.

quote-card-formats.title: Quote Card layouts and social formats
quote-card-formats.body: Quote Card now has stripe, centered, and large-mark layouts, plus square, Facebook landscape, and 9:16. Starter chips load a bargaining, solidarity, or member quote.

portal-solidarity-names.title: Local Portal names in solidarity
portal-solidarity-names.body: Together is home. Hold the line shows which Circles are live. One fight tracks stuck versus moving work, and Many hands is the shared card wall. Committee Circles can open those tools even when they start empty.

comms-stay-free.title: Comms stay free
comms-stay-free.body: The solidarity page now says it plainly: public tools stay free on your device. If we host Officer Hub or Local Portal, hosting has a cost. You can still run the software yourself.

photo-consent-howto.title: Photo consent now names the union risk
photo-consent-howto.body: The Photo Consent guide now covers three event settings and a take-it-down-now rule, so members who need to stay off camera stay protected.

email-outreach-howto.title: Email guide rewritten as a how-to
email-outreach-howto.body: The Email & Member Outreach Guide now covers when email is the official record, how to write a subject members will open, and how to protect addresses with BCC and personal inboxes.

opseu-membership-sector.title: OPSEU / SEFPO membership links follow your sector
opseu-membership-sector.body: College Support still gets Full-Time and Part-Time application links in Brand Kit. Other OPSEU / SEFPO sectors get one All members link to the OPSEU / SEFPO membership form.

graphic-portrait.title: Graphic Maker portrait for Reels
graphic-portrait.body: Graphic Maker can export a tall 9:16 still for Reels, Shorts, and Stories, next to landscape and square. The short-form guide explains when a still is enough.

short-form-guide.title: Short-form video guide
short-form-guide.body: A new handbook for filming on a phone, keeping member privacy, and pointing Reels or Shorts at a meeting, petition, or your local site.

website-wordpress.title: WordPress theme from Website Template
website-wordpress.body: Website Template can download a classic WordPress theme of the same local page. WordPress hosting is still unsupported. GitHub Pages remains the usual path.

website-hero-art.title: Website Template header art
website-hero-art.body: The exported local site can use a colour field, three greyscale patterns, or a photo you upload with consent. No member photos ship in the template.

print-guide-howto.title: Print guide rewritten as a how-to
print-guide-howto.body: The Print Communications Guide now covers why print still reaches members social media misses, a three-second glance test for flyers, and printing on a local budget.

workshop-hour.title: Workshop hour that matches the tools
workshop-hour.body: The workshop outline is a timed lunch-and-learn: strategy, a local logo, Social Examples, Graphic Maker, Quote Card, then a website download. A 20-minute Demo Path walks the same stops.

collection-profiles.title: Brand Kit collection profiles
collection-profiles.body: Brand Kit can hold more than one collection when a local covers more than one workplace, with starter names from published union structures.

site-feedback.title: Site feedback form
site-feedback.body: Send an idea, a bug, an accessibility barrier, or a workshop note without opening GitHub. Optional email is for a reply only, never a mailing list.

brand-fonts.title: Brand Kit fonts for makers
brand-fonts.body: Brand Kit now lets you pick headline and body fonts. Graphic Maker, Flyer Maker, and the other makers use those faces on what you download.

flyer-layouts.title: Flyer Maker layouts and paper sizes
flyer-layouts.body: Flyer Maker gained stack, colour-band, split, and photo-hero layouts, plus letter, half-letter, and tabloid paper. Optional QR and a photo with consent can sit on the same flyer.

local-portal.title: Local Portal for members
local-portal.body: Signed-in members land on Together: Circles, a week digest, and bulletin items, without an empty Officer Hub dashboard.

visual-system.title: A shared look across boards and graphics
visual-system.body: Board notices, flyers, and social graphics now share Brand Kit spacing, lettering, and QR codes, so a set of materials looks like one local.

brand-assets-unions.title: Brand Assets for every union
brand-assets-unions.body: Brand Assets now shows colours and starter files from your Brand Kit union, not only the reference college pack.

seniority-worksheet.title: Seniority worksheet download
seniority-worksheet.body: Document Generator can download a seniority worksheet for stability committees. It is a paper aid, not a bumping calculator.

rtr-pocket-card.title: Right-to-refuse pocket card
rtr-pocket-card.body: QR Link Cards gained a right-to-refuse reference card you can print for stewards. Ontario OHSA only, and not legal advice.

email-outreach-guide.title: Email and member outreach guide
email-outreach-guide.body: Copy-only meeting invites and officer reminders. UnionOps keeps no marketing lists and sends no mail for you.

first-week-print.title: Print step on First week
first-week-print.body: The First week roadmap now includes print after union boards and before social posts, so a flyer is part of the same message as the board and the graphic.

org-chart-directory.title: Org Chart list layouts + blank LEC Word sheet
org-chart-directory.body: Print a poster, a Position | Name list, or a list with campus codes. Need a blank branded Word table? Document Generator has an LEC directory template that does not pull your on-device names.

steward-meeting-guides.title: Steward meeting guides
steward-meeting-guides.body: Three on-device workspaces — five-point filter diagram, Meiorin and work-hardening visuals, pocket PDFs in each tool, and practice links from the steward playbooks hub.

local-bylaws-guide.title: Local Bylaws — definitive floor guide
local-bylaws-guide.body: Diagrams for document hierarchy, amendment flow, and quorum tiers; a worked GMM table; printable adoption and quorum PDFs; and peer constitution sources.

local-bylaws-builder.title: Bylaw Builder — presets, drafts, and exports
local-bylaws-builder.body: Fill sample local sizes, save a draft on this device, then copy, print, or export Markdown, PDF, or text for Word.

bargaining-lifecycle-guide.title: The Bargaining Lifecycle: From Survey to Signing
bargaining-lifecycle-guide.body: A full Local Bargaining Committee playbook — LRA vs college sector, blackout vs updates, No Board countdown, strike-vote and ratification mechanics, failure modes, and the on-device Proposal Tracker.

proposal-tracker.title: Proposal Tracker — keep strategy on your device
proposal-tracker.body: Track articles, union proposals, and employer counters in a spreadsheet on this browser. Export CSV to a USB drive after each session.

guides-tools-menu-ia.title: Clearer Guides and Tools menus
guides-tools-menu-ia.body: Guides now lead with Start here, Steward work, By channel, and Libraries & about — open Steward playbooks for every floor guide. Tools keep five job groups, including Steward prep.

guide-pdf-branding.title: Branded pocket sheets and learning printouts
guide-pdf-branding.body: Officer Learning sheets, bylaws checklists, certificates, and steward workspace PDFs now carry the UnionOps mark so floor printouts look like yours — not a blank Helvetica dump.

office-worksheet-docx.title: Word worksheets for seniority and grievance intake
office-worksheet-docx.body: Document Generator now exports seniority bumping and 6 W's intake sheets as branded Word files—with your Brand Kit fonts bundled so they open correctly offline.

hub-docx-brand-kit.title: Minutes and ballot exports use Brand Kit
hub-docx-brand-kit.body: Meeting minutes and election ballot Word exports now pick up your Brand Kit typefaces, primary colour, and logo when you download from the Officer Hub.

guide-pdf-brand-fonts.title: Pocket sheets use your Brand Kit typefaces
guide-pdf-brand-fonts.body: Officer Learning and bylaws PDFs now pull headline and body fonts from Brand Kit, follow English or French from the site language, and keep the UnionOps mark on every page.

logo-on-brand-fills.title: Logos stay readable on brand-coloured backgrounds
logo-on-brand-fills.body: Meeting backgrounds and other canvas tools keep your mark readable on coral, gold, or other Brand Kit fills — official Looks use the matching plate lockup; your uploaded logo sits on a white card so every colour stays visible.

installPage.title: Install UnionOps as an app
installPage.intro: Add UnionOps to your home screen or taskbar. No app store, and no extra download beyond the browser you already have.
installPage.whyHome: Open it in one tap from your home screen or taskbar, in its own window.

installPage.iosStep1: Open this site in Safari. Chrome on iPhone cannot add the app.
installPage.iosStep2: Tap the Share button (square with an arrow pointing up).
installPage.iosStep3: Scroll down and tap Add to Home Screen.
installPage.androidStep3: Tap Install app. If you only see Add to Home screen, that makes a shortcut, not the full app — use Install when it appears.
installPage.desktopStep2: On the right side of the address bar, click the Install icon (a computer with a down arrow).
installPage.desktopStep3: Confirm. If you do not see Install, you may already be in the app window.
installPage.desktopSafari: On a Mac in Safari, use File, then Add to Dock. Safari never shows an automatic prompt.
installPage.privacyBody: UnionOps does not collect personal data or extra device permissions when you install. The app runs in your browser on this device.
installPage.troubleBody: Use unionops.org, not www. You may already be in the app window. Safari never shows an automatic prompt — follow the steps above. After you change Brand Kit colours, reopen the app (or install it once more) if the icon still looks old.

rtwAccommodation.subtitle: Capture functional limits and proposed measures before you meet HR — notes stay on this device.

legal.primacyBody: Human rights legislation has quasi-constitutional status. It supersedes collective agreements and employer policies when they conflict. If a contract clause blocks a required accommodation, that clause cannot stand against the Code.
legal.meiorinStep1Body: Was the standard adopted for a purpose rationally connected to performing the job?
legal.meiorinStep2Body: Was it adopted in an honest, good-faith belief that it was necessary to achieve that work-related purpose?
legal.meiorinStep3Body: Is the standard reasonably necessary? The employer must show it is impossible to accommodate the individual without imposing undue hardship.
legal.undueHardshipBody: Only three factors may support an undue-hardship claim:
legal.undueHardshipCost: Quantifiable cost so substantial it threatens the nature or viability of the operation
legal.undueHardshipFunding: Outside sources of funding — have grants, insurance, or other programs been explored first?
legal.undueHardshipSafety: Health and safety — objective, evidence-based risk that cannot be mitigated
legal.undueHardshipNotBody: Co-worker morale, customer preference, and conflict with the collective agreement are not undue hardship.

suggestions.heading: Early-resolution suggestions
suggestions.workHardening: Propose a gradual work-hardening schedule: Week 1–2 at 15 hrs, Week 3–4 at 22.5 hrs, Week 5–6 at 30 hrs, then full hours — tied to functional abilities, not diagnosis.
suggestions.taskBundling: Propose task bundling within the current classification so pre-injury wages and bargaining-unit standing stay protected, instead of reclassification into a lower-paid non-unit role.
suggestions.jointReview: Propose a 30-day joint review clause so temporary measures can be tested and adjusted without locking in permanent change or filing a formal grievance yet.

We propose acknowledging the order, documenting the safety or emergency concern, exchanging a mutual apology where appropriate, and resetting expectations without jumping the progressive ladder.

runningMeetingsGuide.title: Running a Meeting & Robert's Rules
runningMeetingsGuide.subtitle: Parliamentary procedure for union meetings — scaled to the room, not a national convention
runningMeetingsGuide.intro: A union meeting without structure is just a shouting match. To ensure everyone gets a fair say and business actually gets done, the labour movement uses Parliamentary Procedure — most commonly Robert's Rules of Order.

disclaimer.title: Not legal advice. Confirm your local rules.
disclaimer.body: Many locals adopt Robert's Rules by reference in their bylaws; some use a simplified standing order. Read your bylaws and any national constitution rules before you chair a general membership meeting.

formality.title: The level of formality
formality.intro: You do not need to run every meeting like a National Convention. Scale your formality to the size of the room:

executive.label: The Executive Meeting (5–10 people)
executive.content: Highly informal. The Chair can make motions, people can speak multiple times, and decisions are often made by consensus ("Are we all good with this?").

gmm.label: The General Membership Meeting (GMM) (20–100 people)
gmm.content: Formal. Members must raise hands, wait to be recognized by the Chair, and motions must be formally moved and seconded. The Chair remains neutral and does not debate.

convention.label: The Convention (500+ people)
convention.content: Extremely formal. Microphones are strictly timed, points of order are tightly regulated, and the rulebook is followed to the letter.

chair.title: The role of the Chair
chair.intro: The Chair (usually the Local President) is the referee, not a player.

referee.label: Keep order
referee.content: The Chair's job is to keep order, manage the speakers list, and ensure the rules are followed.

neutral.label: Stay neutral
neutral.content: The Chair does not debate on motions they are presiding over.

stepDown.label: Step down to debate
stepDown.content: If the Chair wants to passionately debate a motion, they must step down from the chair and let the Vice-President run the meeting until the vote is over.

recognize.label: Recognize speakers
recognize.content: Call on members in the order they rose. State the motion clearly before debate begins: "It is moved and seconded that…"

chair.tip: When in doubt, recognize the member who rose first — then enforce one speaker at a time.

quorum.title: Quorum before you vote
quorum.intro: No binding vote happens without quorum. Your local bylaws define the number — confirm it before you gavel in.

check.label: Open with a count
check.content: The Secretary or Chair records members present. For a GMM, compare the head count to the quorum threshold in your bylaws.

lost.label: Lost quorum mid-meeting
lost.content: If members leave and you drop below quorum, announce it and stop binding votes. You may still hear reports or set a date to reconvene.

special.label: Special meetings
special.content: Bylaw amendments and officer removals often need higher notice and quorum. Read the exact article before you post the notice.

quorum.warning: A motion passed without quorum can be challenged later — even if everyone in the room agreed.

agenda.title: The standard agenda (order of business)
agenda.intro: Most local meetings follow this flow:

items.callToOrder: Land acknowledgement (when your federation or local requires it), then Call to Order & Reading of the Statement of Respect/Solidarity
items.landAckNote: Many Ontario unions — including OPSEU / SEFPO — open with a land acknowledgement before the Statement of Respect and all other business. Research whose territory you are on; the guide below explains federation practice without offering a copy-paste script.
items.minutes: Adoption of the Previous Meeting's Minutes
items.newBusiness: New Business (where new motions are debated)

motion.title: The life of a motion
motion.intro: A motion is a proposal for the local to take action. It follows this path:

move.label: Move
move.content: "I move that we donate $500 to the food bank."

second.label: Second
second.content: "I second the motion." (If there is no seconder, the motion dies instantly.)

debate.label: Debate
debate.content: The Chair asks for debate. The mover gets to speak first.

vote.label: Vote
vote.content: The Chair calls the question. "All in favor? All opposed?"

result.label: Result
result.content: The Chair declares the motion passed or defeated.

precedence.title: Which motion comes first?
precedence.intro: When several motions are on the floor, Robert's Rules ranks subsidiary motions. The Chair must handle the highest-ranking pending motion before returning to debate on the main motion.

adjourn.label: Adjourn
adjourn.body: End the meeting now (if no higher motion is pending).

recess.label: Recess
recess.body: Short break — members stay in the room or return at a set time.

question.label: Previous question (call the question)
question.body: Stop debate and vote immediately — needs two-thirds.

table.label: Table / postpone
table.body: Park the main motion until a later meeting.

limit.label: Limit or extend debate
limit.body: Cap speakers or extend time — specify minutes in the motion.

refer.label: Refer to committee
refer.body: Send the main motion to a committee with instructions and a report-back date.

amend.label: Amend
amend.body: Change wording on the main motion before the final vote.

main.label: Main motion
main.body: The underlying proposal — debated and voted on last.

precedence.caption: Top of the list is decided first. Use the cheat sheet tool for exact wording on each action.
precedence.tip: When someone yells "point of order," stop and rule before you take the next subsidiary motion.

debate.title: Fair debate on the floor
debate.intro: Debate keeps the room focused on the motion — not personalities.

recognize.label: One speaker at a time
recognize.content: Members speak only when recognized by the Chair. Side conversations are out of order.

mover.label: Mover speaks first
mover.content: The member who moved gets the first speech in debate. The seconder does not have to speak.

alternate.label: Alternate sides
alternate.content: Good Chairs alternate for/against when possible so debate stays balanced.

time.label: Time limits
time.content: Many locals limit speeches to two or three minutes at GMM. The Chair can entertain a motion to limit debate.

decorum.label: Stay on the motion
decorum.content: Debate must address the motion on the floor — not unrelated grievances or personal attacks.

voting.title: How votes are taken
voting.intro: The Chair states the question, then members vote. Record the result in the minutes.

voice.label: Voice vote
voice.content: "All in favor? All opposed?" Fast and common for routine items.

hands.label: Show of hands
hands.content: Use when the voice vote is unclear or when your bylaws require it.

ballot.label: Ballot vote
ballot.content: Secret ballot for elections and sensitive decisions — follow your bylaws.

majority.label: Majority
majority.content: Most main motions pass with a majority of votes cast (more than half).

twoThirds.label: Two-thirds
twoThirds.content: Required for previous question, bylaw amendments, and other high-stakes actions — confirm your threshold.

failures.title: When meetings go off the rails
failures.intro: These failures show up in every local eventually. Name them early and correct course.

noSecond.label: No seconder
noSecond.content: Without a second, the motion dies. The Chair should say so clearly and move on.

chairDebates.label: Chair debates
chairDebates.content: If the President argues from the chair, any member can raise a point of order.

lostQuorum.label: Lost quorum
lostQuorum.content: Stop binding votes. Announce the shortfall and adjourn or continue with non-binding discussion only.

wrongOrder.label: Wrong precedence
wrongOrder.content: If someone moves to amend while a motion to table is pending, rule on the table motion first.

friendly.label: "Friendly amendment" myth
friendly.content: There is no friendly amendment without the floor's consent. An amendment still needs a motion, second, and vote.

scenario.title: Worked example: food bank donation
scenario.intro: A member wants the local to donate $500 to the food bank at a general membership meeting. Here is how a well-run floor handles it:

s1.label: New business
s1.content: Chair recognizes Member A under New Business.

s2.label: Main motion
s2.content: Member A: "I move that Local ___ donate $500 to the campus food bank this month." Member B seconds.

s3.label: Debate opens
s3.content: Chair: "It is moved and seconded that… Is there debate?" Member A speaks in favor; Member C speaks against.

s4.label: Amendment
s4.content: Member D: "I move to amend by striking '$500' and inserting '$300'." Debate returns to the amendment first.

s5.label: Vote on amendment
s5.content: Amendment passes. The main motion is now $300 — debate can continue on the revised wording.

s6.label: Final vote
s6.content: Chair: "All in favor of the motion as amended? All opposed?" Motion passes; Secretary records the decision and follow-up task for the Treasurer.

scenario.tip: Open the Rules of Order cheat sheet on your phone when amendments and points of order start stacking up.

tool.title: Mini cheat sheet + full toolkit
tool.intro: Use these together: the guide for training, the cheat sheet live on the floor, and the pocket PDF when you are chairing without Wi‑Fi.

items.pocketPdf: Quorum & motion template PDF — blank motion lines and quorum checklist from Officer Learning module 4

landAcknowledgementGuide.title: Land Acknowledgement Guide
landAcknowledgementGuide.subtitle: How Canadian unions acknowledge Indigenous lands — and how your local can do it with meaning, not a copy-paste script
landAcknowledgementGuide.intro: Land acknowledgements recognize that every union meeting, workshop, and rally in Canada takes place on lands with long Indigenous histories. Major unions — including OPSEU / SEFPO, the Ontario Federation of Labour, CUPE, and BCGEU — pair opening acknowledgements with anti-racism statements, site-specific territory research, and ongoing reconciliation work. This guide explains that practice and helps you prepare your own words. It does not generate text for you.

disclaimer.title: Education, not a shortcut
disclaimer.body: UnionOps does not provide fill-in-the-blank acknowledgement text. National unions publish frameworks and site-specific examples — read those sources, learn from Indigenous nations and knowledge keepers in your area, and write words you can stand behind.

why.title: Why land acknowledgements matter
why.intro: A land acknowledgement is a moment of respect — not a checkbox. It names whose traditional territory you are on and reminds the room that Indigenous peoples are still here.

presence.label: Historical and ongoing presence
presence.content: Indigenous nations have governed, cared for, and lived on these lands since time immemorial. Colonization disrupted that continuity, but Indigenous communities, languages, and governance persist today.

treaties.label: Treaties and agreements
treaties.content: Ontario alone is covered by dozens of treaties and Crown purchases between 1781 and 1930. Many other provinces have their own treaty histories. An acknowledgement opens the door to learning what those agreements mean where you live and work.

reconciliation.label: Reconciliation as practice
reconciliation.content: After the Truth and Reconciliation Commission report, many settler institutions — including unions — began opening meetings with land acknowledgements. Words matter only when they connect to how your local shows up afterward.

beyondToken.label: Moving beyond tokenism
beyondToken.content: OPSEU / SEFPO facilitator guidance warns that acknowledging injustice without a real commitment to repair sounds like an empty apology Indigenous people have heard too often. Personal reflection and accurate research are the minimum respectful starting point.

labour.label: The house of labour's role
labour.content: Unions benefit from colonial structures while Indigenous workers face ongoing discrimination in hiring, health care, and public services. Acknowledging territory is one step toward repairing that relationship — alongside bargaining, solidarity, and Indigenous-led organizing.

why.tip: If you would not say it to an Elder or knowledge keeper in your community, do not say it to a room.

principles.title: Core principles
principles.intro: Four commitments shape a meaningful acknowledgement:

reflection.label: Personal reflection and intentionality
reflection.content: Ask why you are speaking, what you have learned, and what you are willing to do differently because of that learning. Generic language without personal meaning reads as performance.

territory.label: Learn whose traditional territory you are on
territory.content: Research the nations, treaties, and languages connected to the place where your local meets, works, and organizes. Maps and federation guides are starting points — confirm details with Indigenous sources.

action.label: Commit to action alongside the statement
action.content: Pair words with concrete steps: supporting Indigenous-led campaigns, bargaining reconciliation language, donating to Indigenous organizations, or changing local policy. An acknowledgement without follow-through is an empty gesture.

relationship.label: Build relationships, not just sentences
relationship.content: The OFL encourages affiliates to reach out to local First Nations, Métis, and Inuit communities and Friendship Centres — ask what they need rather than assuming. Acknowledgement is the beginning of that relationship.

whenWhere.title: When and where unions acknowledge land
whenWhere.intro: Practice varies by union, but several patterns appear across the Canadian labour movement:

meetings.label: Local and executive meetings
meetings.content: BCGEU convention delegates asked every local and component to open formal meetings with a territory acknowledgement. Many OPSEU / SEFPO locals read one at the start of general membership and executive meetings.

events.label: Conventions, trainings, and rallies
events.content: National and provincial union events typically acknowledge territory at the opening plenary. OPSEU / SEFPO event guides require it at the start of all official functions, alongside the Statement of Respect.

comms.label: Newsletters, websites, and social posts
comms.content: Some locals add a brief acknowledgement to printed materials or event pages. Keep it accurate to where the event physically takes place — not where your web host's servers sit.

virtual.label: Online and hybrid gatherings
virtual.content: Virtual meetings still warrant acknowledgement. OPSEU / SEFPO and other unions use a distinct online wording that recognizes participants may be on different territories while still naming the steward's home land.

everyone.label: Even without Indigenous members
everyone.content: CUPE's reconciliation guides recommend locals move forward even when no member has self-identified as Indigenous. Building relationships with Indigenous workers and communities strengthens the whole union.

unionPractice.title: How major unions approach land acknowledgement
unionPractice.intro: Each national or provincial body publishes its own guidance. Use your federation's materials as the floor — then personalize for your campus, hospital, or shop floor.

opseu.label: OPSEU / SEFPO
opseu.content: Official event facilitator guides require a land acknowledgement and Statement of Respect at the start of every OPSEU / SEFPO function. The acknowledgement goes first on the agenda — before the Statement of Respect and before O Canada. Facilitators use a national framework plus site-specific territory lines for Ontario regions (London, Ottawa, Toronto Head Office, Sudbury, Thunder Bay, and others). If your city is not listed, research using the OFL Ontario guide or Native-Land.ca. Bilingual reading in English and French is recommended. The Indigenous Circle leads the union's reconciliation work — contact them through the Equity Unit before assuming what your local should say.

ofl.label: Ontario Federation of Labour (OFL)
ofl.content: The OFL Traditional Territory Acknowledgements in Ontario PDF provides a sample framework and city-by-city territory lines reviewed by the OFL Aboriginal Circle. It stresses that acknowledgement is only the beginning: read the TRC report, outreach to Friendship Centres, bargain employment equity, and sponsor Indigenous advocacy. Affiliated unions — including OPSEU / SEFPO locals — use this when they need Ontario site-specific language.

cupe.label: CUPE
cupe.content: Walking the Talk explains that land acknowledgements open most CUPE meetings and can include history, ongoing colonial harm, and proper traditional nation names. Locals may invite an Elder or Chief from the territory — with nation-specific protocols — or ask the CUPE National Indigenous Council for guidance. The separate Truth and Reconciliation Bargaining Guide includes sample contract language on acknowledgements, Indigenous sovereignty, non-discrimination, leave, and Elder inclusion at grievance meetings.

bcgeu.label: BCGEU
bcgeu.content: After a 2017 constitutional convention resolution, BCGEU published a First Nations Acknowledgement, Protocol and Terminology guide covering territory statements, tiered acknowledgements (territory first, then ongoing struggles for justice), Elder invitations, and terminology. Locals outside BC can use it as comparative reading for structure and respect.

others.label: Other unions and federations
others.content: Unifor, PSAC, USW, and provincial federations across Canada have increasingly integrated territorial acknowledgement and reconciliation into conventions and education. Check your national union's equity or human-rights page, Indigenous council, or steward school materials — and the Canadian Labour Congress education catalogue for cross-union resources.

unionPractice.tip: National union text is a starting framework. OPSEU / SEFPO explicitly asks facilitators to adapt it with a heartfelt, site-accurate message — not read slides unchanged.

agenda.title: Where it goes on the agenda
agenda.intro: Order signals priority. Several Ontario unions treat acknowledgement as the first business of the gathering:

order.label: First item
order.content: OPSEU / SEFPO event guides place land acknowledgement first — before the Statement of Respect, before national anthem, and before any other business. Treat it as opening ceremony, not an afterthought before lunch.

respect.label: Pair with Statement of Respect
respect.content: OPSEU / SEFPO reads the Statement of Respect immediately after the acknowledgement. It commits the room to anti-harassment and inclusion for all members, including First Nations, Métis, and Inuit peoples. Event coordinators must list at least two qualified contacts for concerns, including one woman.

bilingual.label: English and French
bilingual.content: OPSEU / SEFPO recommends reading the acknowledgement in both official languages when your audience includes Francophone members — especially at provincial or national events.

plenary.label: Breakouts after plenary
plenary.content: If acknowledgement and Statement of Respect were read at opening plenary, facilitators should remind workshop groups the respect commitment remains in effect for the whole event.

facilitator.label: Chair or designated speaker
facilitator.content: The meeting chair, event facilitator, or a member who has done the research usually delivers the acknowledgement. Rotate who speaks so it is not always the same officer reading from memory.

agenda.warning: OPSEU / SEFPO facilitator notes warn against treating acknowledgement as a to-do item to rush through. Pause. Mean it. Connect it to what the meeting will decide.

formats.title: In-person, online, and hybrid formats
formats.intro: The territory you name depends on where people are physically gathered — or where each participant works and lives.

inPerson.label: In-person meetings
inPerson.content: Name the specific nations and treaties for the room you are in. OFL and OPSEU / SEFPO guides include lines such as traditional territory of the Anishinaabeg and Haudenosaunee covered by the Upper Canada Treaties — but only when that matches your location.

online.label: Online meetings
online.content: OPSEU / SEFPO provides separate online guidance: acknowledge that participants join from many lands, name the importance of each person's home territory, and invite reflection on reconciliation. Some locals acknowledge all Indigenous peoples across Turtle Island when the room is fully virtual.

hybrid.label: Hybrid events
hybrid.content: Acknowledge the physical host location first, then recognize that remote participants may be on other territories. Avoid pretending everyone is in one place when they are not.

personalize.label: Adapt, do not photocopy
personalize.content: Every major union guide says the same thing: use the federation framework as a basis, then add accurate site-specific nation and treaty names and a sincere personal sentence about why acknowledgement matters to your local.

learn.title: Learning whose land you are on
learn.intro: Start with reliable tools and federation guides, then go deeper with the nations themselves.

research.label: Use vetted research tools
research.content: Native-Land.ca, Whose Land, the OFL Ontario PDF, and Crown–Indigenous Relations treaty pages help identify nations and agreements. Treat them as introductions, not final authority.

elders.label: Listen to Indigenous voices
elders.content: Seek teachings from Indigenous educators, authors, and community leaders — especially those from the territory you are acknowledging. Do not ask Indigenous members to perform gratitude on demand.

accuracy.label: Check names and spellings
accuracy.content: Nation names (Haudenosaunee, Anishinaabeg, Mississaugas of the Credit, Atikameksheng Anishnaabeg), language names, and treaty titles have correct forms. Copy errors from outdated slides disrespect the people you mean to honour.

context.label: Learn local history
context.content: Residential schools, land dispossession, mining without consent, missing and murdered Indigenous women and girls, and boil-water advisories shape the context for every acknowledgement. The National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation is one place to begin.

friendship.label: Friendship Centres and band offices
friendship.content: The OFL recommends outreach to local Native Friendship Centres and First Nations band or tribal council offices. They can confirm territory names and suggest appropriate community partnerships — ask what they need.

learn.resourcesIntro: The sources at the bottom of this page include territory maps, the NCTR, government treaty hubs, and union federation guides (OFL, OPSEU / SEFPO, CUPE, BCGEU). Read them before you draft your own words.

terminology.title: Terminology and naming
terminology.intro: Accurate, respectful language matters. These terms appear often in Ontario union acknowledgement guides:

nations.label: Haudenosaunee and Anishinaabeg
nations.content: Haudenosaunee refers to the Six Nations confederacy (Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, Seneca, Tuscarora). Anishinaabeg covers Ojibway, Odawa, Algonquin, Potawatomi, Mississaugas, and related nations. Use the specific nation when you know it.

treaties.label: Treaty names
treaties.content: Upper Canada Treaties, Robinson-Huron, Robinson-Superior, Treaty 3, Treaty 9, Treaty 20, and Haldimand Tract appear in federation site lists. Name the treaty that actually covers your meeting location.

turtleIsland.label: Turtle Island
turtleIsland.content: A name used by many Indigenous peoples for North America. OPSEU / SEFPO online acknowledgements reference Indigenous people from across Turtle Island when participants join virtually.

dish.label: Dish With One Spoon
dish.content: Toronto and surrounding areas often reference this covenant between the Haudenosaunee Confederacy and the Confederacy of the Ojibwe and Allied Nations — an agreement to share, work, and protect the land together. Use only when historically accurate for your site.

capitalize.label: Capitalize nation names
capitalize.content: CUPE, BCGEU, and OPSEU / SEFPO guides all stress capitalizing First Nations, Métis, and Inuit names as a sign of respect — the same way you would capitalize France or Ontario.

elders.title: Elders, Chiefs, and opening ceremonies
elders.intro: Some union conventions invite an Elder or knowledge keeper to open with a prayer, smudge, or welcome. That is different from a member reading a written acknowledgement — and carries distinct protocols.

when.label: When to invite an Elder
when.content: CUPE and OFL guides describe Elders opening conferences with ceremony when appropriate. This is not required for every local meeting — a thoughtful member acknowledgement may suffice. Match the formality to the event.

invite.label: How to extend an invitation
invite.content: Contact your union's Indigenous Circle or regional human-rights staff first. The OFL Elder guidelines cover invitation, spelling of names, how to address the Elder, and whether tobacco or a gift is appropriate — protocols differ by nation.

protocol.label: Follow nation-specific protocol
protocol.content: Some nations welcome Elder participation at settler events; others see unsolicited invitations as an imposition. Never assume. Ask the Elder or your Indigenous council contact what is appropriate.

honorarium.label: Honoraria and gifts
honorarium.content: OFL guidelines recommend offering tobacco or a gift when requesting help, plus a monetary honorarium and practical gift afterward. Have payment ready at the event — do not mail it weeks later as an afterthought.

notDefault.label: Do not default to Indigenous members
notDefault.content: OPSEU / SEFPO and CUPE both caution against assuming an Indigenous member will write or perform the acknowledgement. Reconciliation labour should not fall on the few Indigenous people in the room unless they choose to lead.

action.title: Committing to action
action.intro: An acknowledgement should point toward what your local does next — not replace that work.

support.label: Support Indigenous creators and organizations
support.content: Fund Indigenous-led initiatives, buy from Indigenous businesses where appropriate, and amplify campaigns led by Indigenous nations — do not speak over them.

learn.label: Keep learning
learn.content: Treat reconciliation as ongoing education for officers and members, not a one-time workshop. Build Indigenous history and treaty literacy into steward training and meeting culture.

relationships.label: Build relationships with care
relationships.content: If your local partners with Indigenous communities, do so with humility, consent, and long-term commitment — not only when a photo opportunity appears.

accountability.label: Hold your local accountable
accountability.content: Record what you promised after an acknowledgement and revisit it. Members should see progress, not the same sentence year after year with no change.

trc.label: Answer the TRC calls to action
trc.content: Read the Truth and Reconciliation Commission's 94 calls to action and identify which ones your local, employer, or provincial government can advance — from education funding to justice for missing and murdered Indigenous women and girls.

action.tip: Write one concrete action your local will take in the next six months — and assign an owner.

bargaining.title: Land acknowledgement and reconciliation in collective agreements
bargaining.intro: Meeting openings are one surface. CUPE's Truth and Reconciliation Bargaining Guide shows locals also embed reconciliation in contract language:

language.label: Acknowledgement and sovereignty clauses
language.content: Sample language recognizes Indigenous sovereignty and supports workplace land acknowledgements where appropriate — confirm with your bargaining committee and national union before proposing.

leave.label: Truth and Reconciliation Day leave
leave.content: CUPE locals have bargained September 30 as a paid holiday or day of education. Even where it is not statutory, your committee can propose paid leave for commemoration and learning.

workforce.label: Representative workforce and anti-discrimination
workforce.content: Bargain targeted hiring, in-service training, and non-discrimination protections for Indigenous workers — reconciliation includes material workplace equity.

elders.label: Elder inclusion at grievance meetings
elders.content: Some CUPE agreements include Elders at grievance or return-to-work meetings where culturally appropriate. This requires employer agreement and nation-specific protocol.

allLocals.label: Every local can start
allLocals.content: CUPE recommends reconciliation bargaining even when no member has self-identified as Indigenous. OPSEU / SEFPO and other unions similarly treat this as collective responsibility, not a niche issue.

nextSteps.title: Call to action
nextSteps.intro: Reading this page is a start. Meaningful acknowledgement work happens in community, over time.

read.label: Read your federation's guide
read.content: Start with your national union's event or reconciliation materials, the OFL Ontario territory PDF if you are in Ontario, and Native-Land.ca or Whose Land for your specific site.

reflect.label: Reflect before you speak
reflect.content: Journal about why acknowledgement matters to you and what your local has done — or failed to do — for Indigenous justice.

followUp.label: Follow up with your executive
followUp.content: Propose a standing opening practice for meetings, a written plan for action, and a review date — not just a new sentence on the agenda.

community.label: Show up in community
community.content: Attend Indigenous-led events, support land-back and rights campaigns where your members agree, and listen more than you speak.

national.label: Contact your union's Indigenous leadership
national.content: OPSEU / SEFPO's Indigenous Circle, CUPE's National Indigenous Council, and parallel bodies in other unions can guide acknowledgements, Elder protocols, and reconciliation priorities — defer to their leadership.

notThis.title: What this guide is not
notThis.intro: UnionOps deliberately does not offer automated acknowledgement text. Respectful practice cannot be reduced to a dropdown — and national unions say the same about their own frameworks.

generator.label: Not a generator
generator.content: There are no fill-in fields, territory pickers, or copy buttons here. Those tools encourage paste-and-forget scripts.

script.label: Not a script to recite blindly
script.content: Even OPSEU / SEFPO's published framework fails if the speaker does not understand every phrase. Write in your own voice after you have done the reading.

once.label: Not a one-time event
once.content: Acknowledging the land at a single annual meeting is not reconciliation. Build ongoing learning and action into how your local operates.

substitute.label: Not a substitute for Indigenous leadership
substitute.content: Non-Indigenous unions should follow Indigenous-led guidance on when and how to acknowledge territory — and defer to Indigenous voices on their own priorities.

burden.label: Not Indigenous members' unpaid labour
burden.content: Do not ask the only Indigenous steward to write everyone's acknowledgement or educate the room on demand. That work belongs to the whole local — especially settler officers.

notThis.warning: If your local reads the same paragraph for years while taking no action on Indigenous justice, members and community partners will notice. Better to say less and do more.

bylawsGuide.title: Local Bylaws: The Rules of Your Local
bylawsGuide.subtitle: How your local chapter runs day to day under the national constitution
bylawsGuide.intro: Your Local Bylaws are essentially the constitution of your specific chapter. While your National or Provincial union (like OPSEU / SEFPO, CUPE, or Unifor) has a main constitution that governs everyone, your Local Bylaws dictate how your specific house is run on a day-to-day basis.

disclaimer.title: Not legal advice
disclaimer.body: This guide explains common local-bylaw practice. Confirm every notice period, voting threshold, and approval step against your own National or Provincial constitution before you amend or adopt bylaws.

gate.title: Pick the right document
gate.intro: Before you rewrite anything, name which rulebook you are changing. Mixing them up is how locals pass "bylaws" that never take effect.

constitution.label: National / Provincial constitution
constitution.content: The supreme rulebook for every local. Local bylaws cannot conflict with it. Amendment routes live at convention, not at your GMM alone.

bylaws.label: Local bylaws
bylaws.content: How this local elects officers, sets quorum, spends money, and runs meetings. Usually need membership notice, a 2/3 GMM vote, and national approval.

policy.label: LEC policy or standing order
policy.content: Day-to-day operating rules the executive can change more easily. Do not use policy to replace election rules, quorum, or cheque signing.

ca.label: Collective agreement
ca.content: The contract with the employer. Grievance clocks and representation rights live here — not in bylaws. See the grievance playbook for those fights.

gate.warning: If the text changes how officers are elected, how money is spent, or how amendments pass, it belongs in bylaws — with notice and membership vote — not in an LEC email.

mustHave.title: What Must Be in Your Bylaws?
mustHave.intro: A strong set of bylaws removes confusion during disputes. Peer guides (especially CUPE's bylaws guide) and most national constitutions expect clear answers on:

executive.label: The Executive Structure
executive.content: Who makes up the Local Executive Committee (LEC)? (e.g., President, Vice-President, Secretary, Treasurer, Chief Steward).

quorum.label: Quorum
quorum.content: How many members must be present at a General Membership Meeting (GMM) to pass a binding motion or spend money? (Usually a fixed number or a percentage of membership).

signing.label: Signing Authorities
signing.content: Which officers may sign union cheques or authorize electronic payments? Always require at least two signatures.

elections.label: Elections
elections.content: How and when are officers and stewards elected? Term length, nominations, ballots, and vacancy rules belong in writing.

meetings.label: Meetings
meetings.content: How often GMMs happen, who may call special meetings, and how members get the agenda and minutes.

finances.label: Finances and trustees
finances.content: Fiscal year end, financial reports to members, and who audits or reviews the books (often elected trustees).

amendments.label: Amendment clause
amendments.content: Notice period, GMM vote threshold (usually 2/3), and any national approval step before changes take effect.

mustHave.tip: If a dispute arrives and the bylaws are silent, the room invents a rule under pressure — write the answers down while things are calm.

amend.title: How to Amend Bylaws
amend.intro: You cannot just change the rules behind closed doors. Amending bylaws typically requires:

notice.label: Notice
notice.content: You must provide advance notice to the membership (usually 15 to 30 days) that a bylaw amendment will be voted on.

gmm.label: The GMM
gmm.content: The vote must take place at a General Membership Meeting with quorum.

threshold.label: The Threshold
threshold.content: Passing an amendment usually requires a two-thirds (2/3) majority vote of the members present, not just a simple 50%+1.

approval.label: Approval
approval.content: In unions like OPSEU / SEFPO, CUPE, and Unifor, amended bylaws usually need national or provincial officer approval before they take effect.

amend.warning: An LEC vote alone does not amend bylaws. Members need notice, a quorate GMM, and — where your constitution requires it — national approval before the new text is live.

scenario.title: Worked example: raising GMM quorum
scenario.intro: Fictional Local 243 wants to raise GMM quorum from 15 members to 25. Walk the file like an officer, not like a hallway chat.

d0.label: Day 0 — Read the constitution
d0.content: President and Secretary pull the national constitution article on local bylaws and the current Local 243 amendment clause (notice days + 2/3).

d1.label: Day 1 — Draft the change
d1.content: They open Bylaw Builder in Committee draft mode, load the OPSEU / SEFPO college sample, paste the current bylaws for a redline summary, and rewrite only the quorum article. Notes stay on-device for the working group.
d1.artifact: Bylaw Builder committee draft + redline summary

d2.label: Day 2 — Book the GMM
d2.content: They set a GMM date at least 30 days out, post a Board Notice, and send an email with the exact proposed wording.
d2.artifact: Board Notice + member email with exact wording

d3.label: Day 15 — Answer questions
d3.content: At the LEC meeting they record questions from members. They do not "fix" the posted wording without a fresh notice clock.

d4.label: Day 30 — Quorate GMM vote
d4.content: Secretary counts members present against the current quorum rule. The motion needs two-thirds of those present. Minutes capture the count and the result.
d4.artifact: Signed GMM minutes with count and 2/3 result

d5.label: Day 31 — Submit for approval
d5.content: They send the amended bylaws package to the national or provincial office using the path their union requires (often through the members tools hub or national president's office).

d6.label: After approval — Publish
d6.content: Only after written approval do they update the local website, board binder, and member PDF. Until then, the old quorum still governs.

comparePeers.content: Skim a peer guide (CUPE bylaws guide or your own national model) for missing articles.

draftText.content: Draft clean article text in Bylaw Builder Committee mode or Word — one change list members can read aloud.

postNotice.content: Post and send the required advance notice with the exact wording and GMM date.

quorumMath.label: Write quorum math

gmmVote.label: Hold the GMM vote

submitNational.label: Submit for approval
submitNational.content: Submit the package for national/provincial approval when your constitution requires it.

publishMembers.label: Publish to members
publishMembers.content: Publish the approved text to members and retire the old PDF from boards and the website.

examples.title: What other unions publish
examples.intro: You do not need to invent structure from scratch. Open the Sources list at the bottom for live PDFs, then use these notes as a map.

cupe.label: CUPE
cupe.content: A Guide to Preparing Local Union Bylaws walks required provisions and options. The National Constitution Article 12.3 and Appendix B say additional bylaws need National President approval in writing before they take effect.

unifor.label: Unifor
unifor.content: The Unifor Constitution (Article 15) governs Local Unions. The National Executive Board reviews local by-laws and may withhold approval when they conflict with the constitution or equity principles.

opseu.label: OPSEU / SEFPO
opseu.content: Locals follow the OPSEU / SEFPO constitution and send amended local bylaws through the national office path listed on the Members tools hub. Confirm the current PDF there — deep links move when the national site reorganizes.

shared.label: Shared pattern
shared.content: Across these unions: membership notice, a quorate meeting vote (often 2/3), two signing officers, and national review before the new text is live.

examples.tip: Borrow structure from peer guides. Never paste another local's officer names, dues rates, or unit lists into your draft.

failureModes.title: Common ways bylaw work fails
failureModes.intro: Name the failure mode early so the LEC does not "fix it in the hallway" after the vote.

lecOnly.label: LEC-only rewrite
lecOnly.content: Executive votes to change quorum or elections without membership notice. Members can challenge the result; national may refuse approval.

policyAsBylaw.label: Policy dressed as bylaws
policyAsBylaw.content: Spending and election rules live only in an LEC policy binder. When conflict comes, nobody can prove the democratic path.

noNotice.label: Moved goalposts after notice
noNotice.content: Wording on the floor differs from the posted notice. Restart the notice clock or vote only on the posted text.

conflict.label: Conflicts with the constitution
conflict.content: Local text undercuts national election, dues, or equity rules. Constitution wins — rewrite before you waste a GMM.

noApproval.label: Treating GMM passage as final
noApproval.content: Local posts "new bylaws" the next morning without the required national letter. Old bylaws still govern until approval lands.

boardNotice.content: Print the GMM date, time, and "bylaw amendment on the agenda" line for cork boards.

runningMeetings.label: Running meetings guide
runningMeetings.content: Chair a quorate GMM with Robert's Rules — precedence, debate, and the Rules of Order cheat sheet on your phone.

orgChart.label: Org Chart
orgChart.content: Keep the officer roster that bylaws describe aligned with the names members see on the board and website.

email.content: Copy-only member notice patterns — no marketing lists — for the advance amendment email.

articles.name: Article 1: Name. This organization shall be known as {localName}.
articles.purpose: Article 2: Purpose. The purpose of {localName} is to protect and advance the interests of its members, enforce the collective agreement, and promote solidarity in accordance with the National or Provincial constitution.
articles.membership: Article 3: Membership. Membership shall be open to workers covered by the Local's bargaining certificates who are members in good standing of the National or Provincial union. Rights and obligations of membership follow the National or Provincial constitution and these bylaws.
articles.executive: Article 4: Executive. The Local Executive Committee (LEC) shall consist of the President, {vicePresidents} Vice-President(s), Secretary, Treasurer, and the Chief Steward. The LEC administers the Local between General Membership Meetings.
articles.stewards: Article 5: Stewards. Stewards shall be organized as follows: {stewards}. Stewards represent members in the workplace and report to the Chief Steward and the LEC.
articles.quorum: Article 6: Quorum. Quorum for a General Membership Meeting (GMM) shall be {gmmQuorum}. Quorum for an LEC meeting shall be {lecQuorum}. No binding motion or expenditure may pass without quorum.
articles.meetings: Article 7: Meetings. The Local shall hold General Membership Meetings as follows: {meetingFrequency}. Special meetings may be called by the President or by petition of members as set out in the National or Provincial constitution and these bylaws.
articles.elections: Article 8: Elections. Officers and stewards shall be elected for terms of {electionTerm}, in accordance with the National or Provincial constitution and these bylaws. Nominations, notice, and ballot procedures shall be published to the membership before each election.
articles.finances: Article 9: Finances. All cheques and electronic payments of the Local shall require signatures or authorizations from {signingOfficers}. The Treasurer shall present financial reports to the membership. The fiscal year ends on {fiscalYearEnd}.
articles.trustees: Article 10: Trustees. The Local shall have {trustees}. Trustees shall review the books and report to the membership as required by the National or Provincial constitution and these bylaws.
articles.committees: Article 11: Committees. The LEC may establish standing and special committees. Committee terms of reference shall not conflict with these bylaws or the National or Provincial constitution.
articles.amendments: Article 12: Amendments. These bylaws may be amended only after {amendmentNotice}, a vote at a quorate General Membership Meeting, and a two-thirds (2/3) majority of members present. Where required by the National or Provincial constitution, amended bylaws take effect only after national or provincial approval.
articles.conflict: Article 13: Conflict with the Constitution. If any provision of these bylaws conflicts with the National or Provincial constitution, the constitution prevails. These bylaws shall be read to give effect to the constitution wherever possible.

opseuArticles.stewards: Article 5: Stewards. Stewards shall be organized as follows: {stewards}. Stewards represent members in the workplace, receive training as provided by the Local, and report to the Chief Steward and the LEC.

opseuArticles.meetings: Article 7: Meetings. The Local shall hold General Membership Meetings as follows: {meetingFrequency}. Special meetings may be called by the President, by the LEC, or by member petition as set out in the OPSEU / SEFPO Constitution and these bylaws.
opseuArticles.elections: Article 8: Elections. Officers and stewards shall be elected for terms of {electionTerm}, by secret ballot where required by the OPSEU / SEFPO Constitution or these bylaws. Nominations, notice, and ballot procedures shall be published to the membership before each election.
